disclaimer: Yield figures for rice, wheat, maize, lentil, and potato (crops) and buffalo and poultry (livestock) are grounded in cited MoALD/NARC/DLS/published-study figures. Cost-of-cultivation/raising figures are grounded for the original 11 enterprises, and price figures for all except maize (see maize's 'sources' field for why reliable current price data doesn't exist). Enterprises added after that first grounding pass (e.g. mung bean) may have some fields still illustrative where no reliable Nepal-specific source exists — this is stated explicitly per field in each enterprise's 'sources' array, including for agronomic facts (zone/season/soil/water/duration), some of which draw on Indian agricultural-science sources where the underlying plant biology is regional rather than Nepal-specific, while every cost/price figure stays Nepal-sourced or is explicitly flagged as ungrounded. See each enterprise's 'sources' field for exact citations, confidence levels, and caveats — several government cost/price figures date to a 2015/16 or 2013/14 survey year and likely understate current 2025/26 prices; some are single-district studies rather than national averages; a few figures are the author's own transparent estimate built from cited component data rather than one direct citation, and are flagged as such. Every number here must still be validated against current local haat bazaar or cooperative prices and your nearest Krishi Gyan Kendra (agriculture knowledge center) before making real financial decisions. A third batch (tea, coffee, large cardamom, banana, turmeric, chickpea, citrus, kiwi) was added from the sibling nepal_agri_ai research project: zones/seasons/yield are grounded in that project's cited MoALD/NTCDB/Coffee-Board/Spices-Board-adjacent research, but cost-of-cultivation was NOT researched for this batch at all and is a rough analogy-based estimate, and price came from a quick, non-exhaustive web search (current wholesale market reports) rather than the deeper multi-source verification used elsewhere in this file — treat this batch's cost figures especially as rough planning placeholders pending real cost-of-cultivation research, not verified figures.

enterprises.name: Rice (Paddy)
notes: Nepal's government announces a support price for paddy most years, which softens price risk
Needs standing water for much of the cycle — Terai-only, not viable in the hills
Common across Jhapa, Morang, Chitwan and other Terai districts
sources: Yield: ~4.2 t/ha assumed for irrigated Terai rice, between Nepal's national average (~3.5 t/ha, MoALD 2079/80) and major Terai rice-district productivity (~4.86 t/ha per district-level study) — corrected down from an earlier uncited 20 quintal/acre guess

Cost: NPR 30,644/ha cash-plus-leased-land cost (~NPR 30,600/acre) for irrigated Terai paddy — Singh, Singh, Mahto & Raj, 'Economic Analysis of Paddy Cultivation in Kapilvastu District of Nepal,' Annals of Agri-Bio Research 29(1), 2024 (n=46 farmers, 2022/23 season). The same study's pure-cash cost (excl. leased land) is lower at ~NPR 21,000/acre; its full-economic-cost basis (incl. imputed family labor and owned-land rent) is higher at ~NPR 56,750/acre — this field uses the middle, cash-basis figure. Corrected down from an earlier uncited NPR 45,000/acre guess

Price: Nepal government minimum support price (MSP) for paddy, FY 2083/84 (2026/27) — NPR 3,660/quintal (coarse) to NPR 3,860/quintal (medium), the most current official figure available. A floor/support price, not necessarily the exact market transaction price, but well-tracked and directly comparable year to year

monthlyCalendar.sourceNote: Nepal-specific: nursery raised ~May, main transplanting on Asar-15 (Rice/Paddy Day, mid-Jun) per Ratopati/Amarnepal, paddy ripens and is harvested in Kartik-Mangsir (Oct-Nov).

enterprises.name: Wheat
notes: Grown widely across both Terai and mid-hills
Rainfed wheat yields noticeably lower than irrigated — factor that into your own estimate
Good rotation crop after rice or maize
sources: Yield: Nepal's national average wheat productivity is ~2.3 t/ha (2156 kg/ha) — corrected down from an earlier uncited 14 quintal/acre guess; irrigated Terai wheat can run somewhat above this national figure

Cost: NPR 68,347/ha (~NPR 27,700/acre), Nepal national average cost of cultivation — Dept. of Agriculture/MRSMP, 'Production Cost & Marketing of Cereal, Cash, Vegetable & Industrial Crops in Nepal,' FY 2072/73 (2015/16). National, not Terai-specific, and roughly a decade old so likely understates current input costs; a 2023 West Nawalparasi (Terai) study found a lower variable-cost-only figure (~NPR 19,000/acre, excludes fixed costs so not directly comparable). Corrected down from an earlier uncited NPR 30,000/acre guess

Price: Nepal government minimum support price (MSP) for wheat, announced April 2026 (FY 2082/83 harvest) — NPR 3,945/quintal, the most current official figure. Max kept at NPR 4,200/quintal to allow for a modest market premium above the floor price

monthlyCalendar.sourceNote: Nepal agronomy trials show optimal sowing around late November (12-27 Nov window), with harvest starting early March and extending into April/May at higher elevations.

enterprises.name: Maize (Makai)
notes: Nepal's single most widely grown cereal — viable from the Terai up into the high-hills
Also sells as poultry/livestock feed, giving it a second local market
More drought-tolerant than rice, works well on rainfed terraces
sources: Yield: Nepal's national maize productivity is 3.15 t/ha (MoALD 2022: 985,565 ha -> 3,106,397 t); nudged upward for Terai since ~73% of national maize area is hill/mid-hill (typically lower-yielding, often rainfed), so blended national average understates Terai potential — corrected down from an earlier uncited 18 quintal/acre guess despite the upward Terai adjustment

Cost: NPR 63,068/ha (~NPR 25,500/acre), Nepal national average cost of cultivation — same MRSMP FY2072/73 (2015/16) report as rice/wheat. National figure, ~decade old, likely understates current costs. Corrected up from an earlier uncited NPR 22,000/acre guess

Price: NOT grounded — kept illustrative. Unlike rice and wheat, Nepal has no government minimum support price for maize (confirmed absence as of 2025/26; a process to establish one has only just begun). Secondary price data conflicts too widely to responsibly single out a figure: the 2015/16 official farm-gate price was NPR 1,640/quintal, while a 2023 trade-association quote for mill-gate feed maize was NPR 3,500-4,500/quintal — nearly a 3x spread depending on year and market level. Left as an illustrative placeholder pending better data rather than picking an unreliable point estimate

monthlyCalendar.sourceNote: Nepal kharif maize (Apni Kheti / general Nepal cropping calendars): sown with monsoon onset (late May-Jun), harvested autumn (Sep-Oct).
Referred to as 'spring maize' in Nepal literature (e.g. Kawasoti, Nawalparasi sowing-date trials on ResearchGate); sown late Feb-Mar, harvested roughly 3-4 months later.

enterprises.name: Millet (Kodo)
notes: Lowest input cost on this list, tolerates poor terraced hill soil
Traditional staple and a roksi (local liquor) ingredient — steady household/local demand
Limited market beyond the local haat bazaar, so treat as subsistence-first, cash-second
sources: Cost: NPR 53,192/ha (~NPR 21,500/acre) for improved-variety rainfed hill millet, averaged across 5 hill districts (Panchthar, Sindhupalchok, Lamjung, Rukum, Bajhang) — Dept. of Agriculture/MRSMP FY2072/73 (2015/16) report. A decade-old government figure for 'improved' varieties, not the fully subsistence local landraces smallholders often actually grow — treat as an upper-bound-ish estimate. Corrected up from an earlier uncited NPR 10,000/acre guess

Price: NPR 3,000-3,150/quintal, derived from the same FY2072/73 government table (farm-gate/market value divided by yield) — the weakest-sourced price in this dataset; a decade old, and no reliable current millet price data was found (one aggregator's NPR 80-100/kg claim and another's implausible NPR 318-1,274/kg figure were both judged unreliable and excluded rather than used)

Monthly growth-stage calendar added via a dedicated quick-research pass (Nepal-specific sources preferred, India/South-Asia fallback where flagged) -- see each monthlyCalendar entry's own confidence and sourceNote fields for per-season-variant grounding.

monthlyCalendar.sourceNote: Nepal finger millet (kodo), the 4th staple crop, is commonly sown/relayed after maize in the hills during Jun-Jul monsoon onset; harvest month inferred as Nov from ~130-day duration since no source gave an explicit Nepal harvest month.

enterprises.name: Lentil (Musuro Dal)
notes: Core of daily dal-bhat — steady household and local market demand
Fixes nitrogen in soil, good rotation crop after rice or maize
Lowest water need among the crops on this list
sources: Yield: Nepal's national lentil productivity rose from 497 kg/ha historically to 1033 kg/ha in recent years — corrected down substantially from an earlier uncited 6 quintal/acre guess, which had overstated real Nepali lentil yields by roughly 40%

Cost: NPR 29,602/ha (~NPR 12,000/acre) — real Terai farmer practice (not the 'improved variety' government assumption, which runs substantially higher at ~NPR 29,000-31,000/acre), from a 2021 field survey of 107 farmers in Bardiya/Kailali — Poudel et al., 'Economics of Lentil Production Under Relay and Conventional Tillage Practice,' Agriculture Development Journal 16, 2022. Closely matches the pre-existing illustrative guess of NPR 12,000/acre — one of the few figures in this file where the original guess turned out close to real data

Price: NPR 10,060/quintal (implied from the same 2021/2022 Terai farmer-practice study) — more recent than the government's FY2072/73 figure (~NPR 7,700-8,500/quintal) and consistent with it once ~5 years of inflation is accounted for

Monthly growth-stage calendar added via a dedicated quick-research pass (Nepal-specific sources preferred, India/South-Asia fallback where flagged) -- see each monthlyCalendar entry's own confidence and sourceNote fields for per-season-variant grounding.

monthlyCalendar.sourceNote: Apni Kheti / Nepal cropping-system sources: mid-October to first week of November is optimal sowing for lentil (musuro) as a winter rabi pulse, maturing in roughly 105-135 days.

enterprises.name: Potato (Aalu)
notes: Often the single highest-value crop mid-hill smallholders grow
Price swings sharply with harvest timing and Kathmandu-market glut — biggest revenue risk on this list
Needs cold storage or a quick sale plan to avoid distress pricing
sources: Yield: ~20 t/ha assumed for reasonable-practice Terai/mid-hill potato (national MoALD average is lower, ~16.7 t/ha, below the ~21 world average; well-managed plots reach 20-25 t/ha) — this is the one figure that was already close to real, unlike the other crops revised in this pass

Cost: NPR 273,232/ha (Terai, ~NPR 110,600/acre) and NPR 261,684/ha (Hills, ~NPR 105,900/acre) — Dept. of Agriculture/MRSMP FY2072/73 (2015/16), cross-validated by an independent 2019 Achham (mid-hills) study at a similar level (~NPR 103,700/acre). This field averages Terai+Hills to ~NPR 108,000/acre; high-hills growing (e.g. Mustang) costs run roughly 2.5x higher (~NPR 267,000/acre per a 2021 Mustang-specific study) due to input-transport costs — a real regional difference this dataset's single-cost-per-enterprise model can't capture. Corrected up substantially from an earlier uncited NPR 60,000/acre guess, which understated potato's genuinely high input cost (seed tubers + fertilizer)

Price: NPR 2,050/quintal (Terai) to NPR 3,033/quintal (Achham mid-hills, 2019, more recent) farm-gate. A high-hills (Mustang, 2021) study found a much higher NPR 5,554/quintal, excluded from this range as unrepresentative of the Terai/hills case this figure primarily targets

Monthly growth-stage calendar added via a dedicated quick-research pass (Nepal-specific sources preferred, India/South-Asia fallback where flagged) -- see each monthlyCalendar entry's own confidence and sourceNote fields for per-season-variant grounding.

monthlyCalendar.sourceNote: Nepal terai/low-hill main winter potato crop: planted Bhadra-Ashwin through autumn into Sep-Dec (Krishi Suchana / FoodSansar), harvested Mangsir-Poush (Nov-Jan) roughly 90 days later.
Mid-hill spring/summer potato crop: planted Magh-Falgun (mid-Jan to mid-Mar) and harvested Baisakh-Jestha (mid-Apr to mid-Jun) per Nepal potato industry overview (PotatoPro/FoodSansar).

enterprises.name: Ginger (Aduwa)
notes: High-value hill cash crop, especially in eastern Nepal (Ilam, Panchthar)
Nepal's classic boom-bust crop — price has crashed hard in past oversupply years
Seed rhizome cost alone is a large share of the input cost — budget for it separately
sources: Cost: NPR 734,082/ha (~NPR 297,000/acre), averaged across 8 hill districts (Terhathum, Palpa, Pyuthan, Khotang, Doti, Kailali, Salyan, Dhankuta) — Dept. of Agriculture/MRSMP, 'Production Cost and Marketing of Pulses, Oilseeds, Spices and Commercial Crops,' FY2072/73 (2015/16). Doesn't include Ilam/Panchthar by name (though Dhankuta/Terhathum are the same eastern-hills ginger belt) — a regional proxy, not an exact match. Seed rhizome alone is ~63% of this cost, matching the crop's known expensive-seed-cost reputation. Corrected up substantially (roughly doubled) from an earlier uncited NPR 150,000/acre guess

Price: NPR 5,000-20,000/quintal — widened dramatically from the earlier illustrative NPR 4,000-7,000/quintal range to reflect real, well-documented Kalimati market wholesale price history: Rs 100-200/kg (2013/14) -> crashed to Rs 50-70/kg (2015-18) -> spiked over Rs 200/kg (2019/20) -> crashed to ~Rs 50/kg (2020-22) -> spiked over Rs 300/kg (mid-2023) -> fell to ~Rs 150/kg (late 2023). Source: CAIDMP/Nepal Agricultural Economics Society ginger trade workshop booklet, 2024. This crop's boom-bust volatility is real and severe, not a modeling artifact — already reflected in its maximum (5/5) priceVolatility risk rating

Monthly growth-stage calendar added via a dedicated quick-research pass (Nepal-specific sources preferred, India/South-Asia fallback where flagged) -- see each monthlyCalendar entry's own confidence and sourceNote fields for per-season-variant grounding.

monthlyCalendar.sourceNote: Multiple Nepal-specific sources (Hananoie Nepal, ginger cultivation guides) agree ginger (aduwa) is planted April-May and harvested December-January, roughly 8-10 months later, matching the 240-day duration.

enterprises.name: Apple (Syaau)
notes: The highest-value crop on this list — a proven transformative cash crop in districts like Mustang and Jumla
This estimate assumes an already-bearing orchard — a new orchard takes 4-5 years before first real harvest
Only viable in cold high-hill climates, not below that elevation
sources: Cost: NPR 223,661/ha (Mustang, ~NPR 90,500/acre) and NPR 227,326/ha (Jumla, ~NPR 92,000/acre) for an established (year 11-15) bearing orchard, matching this enterprise's 'already-bearing orchard' framing — Dept. of Agriculture/MRSMP, 'Production Cost and Gross Profit from Fruit Farming in Nepal,' FY2072/73 (2015/16). High-hills-specific, matching this enterprise's zone restriction. Corrected down from an earlier uncited NPR 120,000/acre guess

Price: NPR 8,000-18,000/quintal — the government source's own embedded farm-gate price (NPR 3,500-3,700/quintal, derived from its income/production tables) is clearly stale: independently-reported Kathmandu wholesale apple prices have since risen sharply, with a 2026-reported Kalimati minimum wholesale price around NPR 28,000/quintal (Rs 280/kg). This range is a deliberately wide bridging estimate between the dated farm-gate figure and recent wholesale reality (farm-gate typically runs below wholesale) — not a single clean citation, and the softest-sourced price correction among the crops in this file

Monthly growth-stage calendar added via a dedicated quick-research pass (Nepal-specific sources preferred, India/South-Asia fallback where flagged) -- see each monthlyCalendar entry's own confidence and sourceNote fields for per-season-variant grounding.

monthlyCalendar.sourceNote: Nepal high-hill apple belts (e.g. Marpha/Mustang) rely on winter chilling for spring bloom and harvest in late summer/early autumn; exact harvest window cross-checked against Himachal Pradesh (July-Oct) as a climatically similar reference since granular Nepal month data was sparse.

enterprises.name: Goat (Khasi/Boka)
notes: Demand and prices spike hard around Dashain — timing sales to the festival matters
Lowest capital and space needs of any livestock on this list
Can be raised alongside crops with minimal land dedicated to it
sources: Cost: NPR 6,214/goat over an 8-month raising cycle — Ghimire et al., 'Factors affecting the profitability from goat farming in Gulmi, Nepal,' Cogent Food & Agriculture 7(1), 2021. Single-district (Gulmi) study; internally consistent with the same study's reported benefit-cost ratio (2.90) against its own revenue figure. Corrected down from an earlier uncited NPR 10,000/goat guess

Price: NPR 18,000/goat sale value — same Gulmi study (matches this field's pre-existing figure exactly), independently corroborated by Feb 2026 Kathmandu Valley wholesale live-weight prices (~NPR 670-755/kg for Terai/hill goats) applied to a ~25kg market-weight goat (per a Gorkha district livestock-office business-plan manual) = ~NPR 17,000-19,000. Max raised to NPR 26,000 to reflect the well-documented Dashain festival price premium (government sources describe festival demand as able to 'double' goat prices), though the exact festival-season live-animal price wasn't as precisely cited as the off-season figure

enterprises.name: Sheep (Bheda, Baruwal)
notes: Not a Terai enterprise -- Baruwal and Nepal's other native breeds are mountain/hill grazing animals, so this entry is zoned hills/high-hills only

Wool (0.3-1.3 kg/sheep/year, used for radi/pakhi/galaicha textiles) is real additional income this entry does NOT model as a second revenue stream -- no reliable Nepal wool price per kg was found to add it honestly

COST AND PRICE HERE ARE BOTH ESTIMATED, NOT DIRECTLY CITED -- see sources below. This is the least-certain economics entry in the whole catalog; treat the profit/ROI numbers as a rough starting order of magnitude, not a real study result
Lowest capital and space needs of any livestock on this list, same as goat -- can be raised alongside crops with minimal dedicated land
sources: Production data (breed, wool yield, weight): Baruwal is Nepal's dominant native sheep breed (63% of the national herd, alongside Bhyanglung 4%, Kage 21%, Lampuchhre 12%), grazed up to ~3,000m -- agrifarming.in "Sheep Farming In Nepal, Breeds, Business Plan". Wool yield 0.3-1.3 kg/sheep/year (native breeds), vs ~3.5 kg for well-fed exotic breeds -- same source. Adult weight is cited inconsistently across sources: this same article gives 40-75 kg (possibly reflecting larger/crossbred stock), while a separate general mountain-livestock profile gives 25-30 kg; this entry uses 25-30 kg since it matches the same small-bodied, extensively-grazed Baruwal system the rest of this entry describes, not the larger figure

Cost: NPR 6,200/sheep over an 8-month cycle -- NOT a direct sheep citation. No Nepal-specific sheep cost-of-raising study was found despite an extensive search (DLS livestock statistics, academic databases, business-plan guides all came up short on a real per-animal cost figure). Carried over directly from this file's own goat entry (NPR 6,214/goat over an 8-month cycle -- Ghimire et al., "Factors affecting the profitability from goat farming in Gulmi, Nepal," Cogent Food & Agriculture 7(1), 2021) on the reasoning that Nepali hill goat and Baruwal sheep are raised under materially the same extensive/semi-intensive grazing system, similar body-size class, and similar cycle length. This is a same-system analogy, not a sheep-specific measurement -- the single weakest-justified cost figure in this entire dataset

Price: NPR 6,000-13,500/sheep sale value -- NOT a direct citation either. Derived by multiplying a live-weight wholesale price range (~NPR 240-455/kg, converted at ~NPR 133/USD from a market-data aggregator's ~US.81-3.42/kg wholesale live-sheep figure, selinawamucii.com, Sept 2026) by this entry's own 25-30 kg Baruwal adult-weight assumption above -- two stacked estimates, not a measurement. The aggregator was cross-checked for plausibility against an independently-found retail mutton price (NPR 364-617/kg, Kathmandu/Pokhara, 2025/26 market data) for the same period and landed in a consistent range, which is why it was kept -- a same-style aggregator gave an implausible duck-meat figure (roughly 5-10x too high) during this same research pass and was discarded instead; this sheep figure passed that same plausibility check but should still be treated as the least certain price in the whole enterprise catalog

enterprises.name: Buffalo (dairy, per animal)
notes: Buffalo milk's higher fat content earns a price premium over cow milk in most Nepali markets
Reliable fodder supply, not land, is usually the real constraint
Margin is thin in a typical year — valued as much for steady cash flow as for profit
sources: Cost: NPR 78,884/year — annual operating cost (feed, care) for one dairy buffalo, Kaski district, Aug-Oct 2024 survey — Pandey et al., 'Production Costs, Profitability, and Challenges in Dairy Farming: Insights from Kaski District, Nepal,' Trends in Agricultural Sciences 4(4), 2025. Corrected down substantially from an earlier uncited NPR 160,000/year guess, which appears to have conflated ANNUAL operating cost with the one-time PURCHASE price of a buffalo (a 2025 Kathmandu Post investigation into a Karnali government buffalo scheme found improved-breed Murrah buffalo purchase prices around NPR 150,000/animal — close to the old guess, but that's a one-time capital cost, not this field's per-year figure)

Yield: ~1,428 liters/lactation — same Kaski 2024/25 study. Cross-checked against other sources: a 2003/04 Chitwan study found 1,932 L/305-day lactation for improved stock, while indigenous hill breeds (Lime, Parkote) run lower at ~1,048 L. Corrected down from an earlier uncited 1,800 L/year guess, which sat toward the higher end of the real range

Price: NPR 75-110/liter — the weakest-sourced figure in this entire dataset. No clean, authoritative Nepal-specific buffalo milk farm-gate rate was found despite extensive searching (one promising-looking figure turned out to be an Indian cooperative's rate, mistakenly indexed as Nepali, and was discarded). Nepal's dairy board publishes a cow-milk baseline of NPR 65/liter (4% fat basis); buffalo milk is consistently described as earning a fat-content premium but no exact NPR rate for that premium was locatable. This range is the author's own triangulated synthesis, not a direct citation — treat with the most caution of any figure in this file

enterprises.name: Poultry (Broiler, per batch)
notes: Fastest cash-cycle on this list — can run several batches a year
Feed cost (often imported maize/soybean) is the main driver of your margin
Disease and heat stress are real risks without basic biosecurity
sources: Cost: ~NPR 115,000-125,000/batch of 300 birds — not a single cited total (no accessible Nepal study reported total batch cost), but a transparent bottom-up estimate from real, cited component prices: day-old Cobb 500 chicks at NPR 70-75/chick, Kathmandu Valley, June 2025 (Nepal Hatchery Industries Association, via myRepublica) = ~NPR 21,000-22,500 for 300 birds; feed at NPR 65-75/kg, ~4kg/bird to reach market weight = ~NPR 78,000-90,000 for 300 birds; remaining NPR 8,000-15,000 covers vaccines/litter/brooding/mortality buffer (the least well-sourced piece). Feed is consistently reported as 65-80% of total broiler cost, consistent with this breakdown. Corrected up from an earlier uncited NPR 90,000/batch guess

Yield: 780 kg liveweight/batch (2.6kg/bird x 300 birds at ~44-day market slaughter age) — Central Bureau of Statistics/National Statistics Office Nepal poultry-sector survey, reference year 2024, reported in The Kathmandu Post, March 2026. Corrected up substantially from an earlier uncited 550kg/batch guess (~1.83kg/bird), which understated real market slaughter weight

Price: NPR 210-230/kg liveweight — centered on NPR 220-224/kg from two independently corroborating current sources: a June 2025 National Chicken Sellers Association quote (NPR 220/kg, Kathmandu Valley) and an independent cross-check derived from official 2024 national production/revenue statistics (NPR 57.86 billion revenue / 258,626 tonnes = ~NPR 224/kg). Corrected down substantially from an earlier uncited NPR 320-380/kg guess, which significantly overstated real broiler prices

enterprises.name: Yak/Chauri (dairy, high-hills)
notes: Requires high-altitude pasture (2,000-6,000m) -- a true high-hills specialist, not viable lower down
Chauri (yak x cattle hybrid females) are the primary dairy animal in most herds -- pure yak (nak) females milk far less

Byproducts beyond milk (ghee, chhurpi/dried cheese) add real income this entry does not model as a separate revenue stream -- chhurpi alone has reportedly earned NPR 80,000-200,000/year for households with 5-15 animals
Herding is typically transhumant (seasonal high-pasture movement) and labor/lifestyle-intensive in a way this economics-only figure does not capture
sources: Yield: 3.45 liters/day for chauri (vs 1.67 L/day for nak/pure yak females) -- "Study on husbandry practices and productive performance of Yak/Chauries in Nepal" (ResearchGate, 2020). Annualized to 828 L/year using an 8-month (~240-day) lactation period, matching this same literature's description of chauri milking "for around eight months per year"
Price: NPR 88-120/liter for nak/chauri milk -- same 2020 husbandry-practices study

Cost: NPR ~43,000/animal/year -- NOT a direct citation, derived by applying a real cost-to-income ratio to the revenue figure above. The ratio itself comes from an older FAO transhumant-grazing-systems report on Thodung chauri herds (Sindhupalchok), which found herders' milk income "barely covers" management/feed/medicine costs, with a separately-cited related figure (FAO chauri production systems, Sindhupalchok) showing roughly half of gross milk income consumed by these costs across a studied 22-chauri herd. This is the weakest-sourced figure in this entry -- an old (likely early-2000s), non-Nepal-current-price-level ratio applied to a newer revenue number, not a real current cost study. Treat with the most caution of any figure in this file

Zone restriction (2,000-6,000m) and Sherpa/high-hills herding context: National Forage & Grassland Research Centre Nepal; Economics of Yak herding in the Kanchenjunga landscape of the Eastern Himalayas, Pastoralism journal, 2023 (60 herders, Panchthar/Taplejung districts) -- this latter study independently describes yak/chauri herding economics as generally marginal ("not financially attractive"), consistent with this entry's thin margin (cost ~50% of revenue)

enterprises.name: Mung Bean (Moong)
notes: Grown as a rice-fallow catch crop: sown after the rabi harvest (wheat/lentil/mustard), harvested before the next kharif rice transplanting — fills the zaid gap between rabi and kharif that no other crop on this list currently covers
Genuine soil-building value, not just a cash crop: fixes real nitrogen that measurably benefits whatever's planted after it
Very short cycle (70-80 days) and low water/capital needs make it a low-risk way to use land that would otherwise sit fallow
sources: Zones/season/water/soil/duration: Terai and hills up to ~1,000m (not high-hills); zaid (Mar-May) is the well-documented primary season, sown mid-March to mid-May as a rice-fallow catch crop — CSISA/CIMMYT Nepal, 'Multiple Benefits from Mungbean Production' brochure (2019), corroborated by a 2025 Rupandehi (western Terai) field trial (Frontiers in Agronomy) sown May 2, and NARC on-farm trials (Khanal et al. 2004/2006). Duration 70-80 days stated explicitly in the Nepal brochure. A secondary kharif planting window is sometimes mentioned in passing but wasn't well-documented enough to include with confidence — zaid is the evidenced season

Nitrogen contribution to the FOLLOWING crop — the reason this entry exists: 30-37 kg N/ha residual benefit, worth roughly 25% of the following cereal's nitrogen fertilizer requirement, cross-validated between an India/Punjab study (Sekhon et al. 2007, cited in Shanmugasundaram/Keatinge/Hughes, 'The Mungbean Transformation,' IFPRI Discussion Paper 00922, 2009) and a Nepal-specific figure (CSISA/CIMMYT Nepal brochure: 30-35 kg N/ha, equivalent to 65-75 kg urea/ha). A real, quantified figure, not just a qualitative 'legumes fix nitrogen' claim — though this app's rotation scorer currently still applies a flat, conservative +8% profit bonus rather than translating the kg-N figure directly into a profit adjustment (see rotation.js)

Cost: NOT grounded — kept illustrative (NPR 13,500/acre, roughly matching lentil's grounded low-input-legume cost as the closest reasonable proxy). Nepal's own cost-of-cultivation report series (MRSMP/CAIDMP 'Pulses, Oilseeds, Spices and Commercial Crops,' FY2072/73 — the same report that grounded lentil/potato/ginger/millet costs) was read in full and confirmed to explicitly NOT include mung bean; its pulses coverage is lentil, pigeon pea, black gram, kidney bean, snow pea, and cowpea only. This is a real, confirmed gap in Nepal's public data, not a search failure

enterprises.name: Sesame (Til)
notes: Often a secondary/fallback oilseed on dry, marginal land not suited to higher-value crops, rather than a primary cash crop — Nepal's own oilseed research program gives it lower breeding priority than mustard or groundnut
Tolerates genuinely poor rainfed conditions where little else grows
Season is honestly uncertain (see sources) — this listing includes both kharif and rabi since the evidence conflicts rather than picking one
sources: Season: GENUINELY CONFLICTING evidence, reported honestly rather than resolved by guessing. The one Nepal GOVERNMENT primary dataset found (Dept. of Agriculture/MRSMP FY2072/73 cost survey, 5 districts) shows sowing in Mangsir (Nov-Dec) and harvest in Magh/Falgun (Jan-Mar) — a rabi pattern. Separate, non-government Nepal agriculture sources describe sowing at monsoon onset (Jestha/Ashadh, ~May-July) — a kharif pattern, the South Asian default. No Nepal source for a zaid/spring planting was found despite targeted searching. Both kharif and rabi are included here pending ground-truthing against a local Krishi Gyan Kendra calendar

Zones/water/soil: Terai and hill districts (Bara, Kapilwastu in Terai; Lamjung, Dailekh, Khotang in hills) all surveyed as rainfed/unirrigated — Dept. of Agriculture/MRSMP FY2072/73 report (Nepal). Soil described only qualitatively ('dry and marginal lands') in the Nepal source; light-to-medium well-drained soil (pH 5.5-8.0) per ICAR/Vikaspedia (India) — used for the soil-type field only, not for cost/price
Duration: 115-120 days per the released Nepal variety 'Nawalpur Khairo Til-1' (National Oilseed Research Program, Nawalpur/Sarlahi) — Nepal-sourced

Cost: NPR 43,242/ha (~NPR 17,500/acre), 5-district Nepal average — same MRSMP FY2072/73 report as ginger/potato/millet. A decade-old figure, likely understates current cost; no more recent Nepal sesame cost survey was found

Yield: 719 kg/ha (~2.9 quintal/acre), same 5-district Nepal survey — notably below the variety's genetic potential (1.2 t/ha trial-station figure), which is normal and expected for real farmer fields vs. research trials

Price: NPR 13,100-15,500/quintal, same Nepal government survey (farmgate to wholesale, per-district). A commercial aggregator (Selina Wamucii, 2026) claims a wildly higher NPR 30,500-63,500/quintal with unclear methodology — excluded as unreliable rather than used

enterprises.name: Jute (Patuwa)
notes: Historically Nepal's single largest cash crop and foreign-exchange earner (up to ~50% of convertible FX in 1979) — the Biratnagar Jute Mill (1936) was Nepal's first modern industrial enterprise, and the 1947 mill strike there is widely credited as a catalyst for Nepal's democracy movement

Sharp, well-documented decline: Morang's jute area has fallen from ~40,000 ha two decades ago to ~5,100 ha today, Sunsari from ~20,000 ha to ~1,300 ha — mainly displaced by sugarcane's better returns plus jute's own high labor cost (>70% of production cost is labor)

Role reversal: Biratnagar's remaining jute mills now import roughly 75% of their raw jute from India/Bangladesh (~NPR 3 billion/year) — the crop that once defined the eastern Terai economy can no longer fully supply its own local industry
Core belt today is specifically Jhapa/Morang/Sunsari on Koshi-floodplain alluvial soil — this is a real, currently-produced Sunsari-district crop, not a historical footnote
sources: Zones/districts: Morang (dominant, ~5,100 ha, ~7,400 t), Sunsari (~1,300 ha, ~2,000-2,080 t), Jhapa (~550 ha), with historical presence in Siraha/Saptari/Ilam/Udayapur — MoALD Statistical Information on Nepalese Agriculture 2079/80, corroborated by The Kathmandu Post (Sept 2026) and Sharesansar.com (Sept 2023) reporting on Koshi Province jute. All Nepal-sourced

Season: kharif, inferred from a Sept 2026 Kathmandu Post report of active Sunsari harvest that month (implying ~April/May sowing), consistent with Indian agronomic sources (CRIJAF/ICAR) giving a Feb-May sowing window and 120-150 day duration for the same crop across the shared Gangetic-plain belt

Water/soil: 'limited irrigation water at sowing' documented as a real production constraint (Agronomy Journal of Nepal, 2013, survey of Jhapa/Morang/Sunsari, 2005/06 season) — both irrigated assistance and rainfed cultivation occur. Soil: alluvial/sandy-loam/clayey per a Nepali agriculture extension portal (krishisuchana.com), matching the Koshi-floodplain geography of the core districts

Cost: GENUINELY UNRESOLVED, reported honestly rather than averaged. A 2013-published study of the 2005/06 season implies ~NPR 11,300-14,300/acre — but that figure is now two decades old. A named Sunsari farmer directly quoted in a Sept 2026 Kathmandu Post story states it costs 'at least NPR 50,000' to grow jute on 5 kattha (~0.42 acre) — implying ~NPR 119,500/acre. This field uses NPR 100,000/acre, weighted toward the recent figure (consistent with the well-documented rising-labor-cost story behind jute's real decline) but rounded down slightly since it rests on a single farmer's account, not a systematic survey — treat with real caution

Yield: 6 quintal raw fiber/acre, weighted toward the more recent and geographically precise 2022-2026 figures (Sunsari 2026: ~6.3 quintal/acre; national FY2079/80: ~5.7-5.9 quintal/acre) over an older, higher 2005/06 eastern-Terai study (~7.2-9.2 quintal/acre) — all Nepal-sourced

Price: NPR 8,300/quintal (2023 low, per Sharesansar/Koshi Province officials) to NPR 15,000/quintal (2026 current, per a Sunsari farmer quoted at NPR 6,000/40kg in the same Kathmandu Post story) — both Nepal-sourced and dated by year, reflecting real documented year-to-year volatility rather than a single averaged figure

enterprises.name: Garlic (Lahsun)
notes: Fits a genuine, distinctive Terai rotation niche: no-till garlic planted directly into residual soil moisture right after monsoon rice harvest, mulched with rice straw — uses the rabi window without displacing the rice crop

Nepal produces real volume (~73,500-75,000 t/year) but is still heavily import-dependent on Chinese garlic (NPR ~6.18 billion imported in just 6 months) — a real domestic-substitution opportunity, not a niche crop
White rot (a soil fungus) can persist 20+ years once established — never follow this with onion or another allium crop on the same land, and only ever use clean seed stock
No single dominant 'garlic belt' the way rice or jute has one — production is dispersed across hill districts plus pockets in Terai and even high-hill areas like Humla and Mustang
sources: Zones: grown up to ~3,000 masl per Nepal agricultural practice; Humla (far-western high-hill district) reported self-sufficient, and Marpha/Mustang (high-hill, ~2,670m) maintains a named local seed variety — Nepal-sourced (Rising Nepal Daily; Temperate Horticulture Development Center, Marpha)

Season: Terai/hills sown Ashoj-Mangsir (Sept-Nov, rabi); a distinct high-hills spring (Feb-Apr) sowing pattern also exists but isn't separately modeled here (this dataset uses one season set per enterprise, not per zone) — Nepal-sourced (agrisujan.wordpress.com), corroborated by Indian ICAR-family guidance for the same Sept-Oct plains sowing window

Water/soil: needs irrigation at sowing and every 10-15 days per standard practice, but a real no-till Terai system relies on residual post-monsoon soil moisture instead (see notes) — Nepal-sourced (ICIMOD no-till garlic technology note) plus Indian ICAR/TNAU package-of-practice guidance for soil preference (avoid heavy clay)
Duration: 130-150 days, Nepal-sourced (agrisujan.wordpress.com) closely matching Indian ICAR-family figures (135-150 days)

Cost: NPR 249,764/ha (~NPR 101,000/acre), 7-district Nepal average — Dept. of Agriculture/MRSMP, 'Production Cost and Marketing of Pulses, Oilseeds, Spices and Commercial Crops,' FY2072/73 (2015/16) — the same report grounding lentil/potato/ginger/millet/sesame. A decade-old figure; this appears to still be the most recent edition of this specific report (checked CAIDMP's current listings; only cereal and fruit cost reports have been updated since)

Yield: 64.35 qtl/ha (~26 quintal/acre), same MRSMP report. Cross-checked against MoALD national statistics FY2079/80 (2022/23): ~76.9 qtl/ha (~31 quintal/acre) nationally, notably higher — plausible given 10 years of improvement, used as corroboration not replacement. A 2015 Kathmandu Post figure of 170-186 qtl/ha (~2.7x higher than either) could not be reconciled with any other source and was excluded rather than used

Price: NPR 11,000-15,000/quintal — blends a decade-old official farm-gate figure (~NPR 7,959-8,299/quintal, MRSMP FY2015/16) with a current Kalimati Fruits & Vegetables Market Development Board wholesale rate for Nepali (not Chinese-imported) dried garlic (~NPR 13,000/quintal, 2025/26, via Ratopati/Desh Sanchar market reports) — weighted toward the more recent figure since Kalimati tracks Nepal-origin garlic specifically

enterprises.name: Mustard/Rapeseed (Tori)
notes: Nepal's dominant oilseed by far — 77% of national oilseed production — and a NARC-validated rice-mustard sequential cropping system exists specifically for Terai conditions, exploiting residual soil moisture right after monsoon rice
Also commonly grown as a bund intercrop alongside wheat, lentil, or chickpea, or as a short-duration relay/catch crop filling the rice-fallow gap before wheat sowing

Its crop residue has a real biofumigation effect (suppresses some soil-borne pathogens/nematodes for a following crop) — a genuine soil-health benefit distinct from nitrogen fixation, which mustard does not provide
Chitwan is a real, currently-expanding mustard belt — surveyed area nearly doubled between 2019/20 and 2023/24
sources: Zones/season: Terai-dominant with hills as a real secondary zone (high-hills evidence too weak to include); sown Ashoj-Mangsir (mid-Sept-Nov, rabi) — Nepal-sourced (MoALD 2022 oilseed statistics; Dept. of Agriculture/MRSMP survey district list), corroborated by Indian ICAR/Vikaspedia guidance for the same sowing window

Water/soil: MRSMP survey covers 'improved and irrigated' mainseason mustard, but rainfed relay-cropping on residual monsoon moisture is also extremely common across the Terai — Nepal-sourced (MRSMP report; rice-fallow cropping-systems literature)

Duration: 'mustard/rapeseed' bundles two real maturity classes — short-duration toria (~75-90 days) and full-season mustard/rayo (~110-140 days); 100 days used as a rough middle estimate, not a single clean citation — India-sourced ranges (ICAR/Vikaspedia) with Nepal cropping-calendar context

Cost: NPR 58,491/ha (~NPR 23,700/acre), 7-district Nepal average — Dept. of Agriculture/MRSMP FY2072/73 (2015/16), same report as garlic/lentil/potato/ginger/millet/sesame. A decade-old figure. A separately-cited 'NPR 1,201,452/ha' figure from a secondary source (~20x every other figure found) could not be verified against its primary source and was excluded as an almost-certain error, not used

Yield: 9.89 qtl/ha (~4.5 quintal/acre) — blends the MRSMP FY2015/16 base figure (9.89 qtl/ha) with two more recent, higher cross-checks suggesting real yield improvement since: national average ~11.1 qtl/ha (2020/21) and a Chitwan-specific ~13 qtl/ha (Kathmandu Post, 2024) — all Nepal-sourced

Price: NPR 11,000-17,000/quintal — Kathmandu Post (Jan 2024), reporting mustard seed price rising from NPR 11,000/quintal (Feb 2022) to NPR 17,000/quintal after the 2022/23 global price spike, since partly receded. Preferred over the decade-old MRSMP price figure (~NPR 9,000-9,300/quintal, FY2015/16) as the more current, decision-useful figure

enterprises.name: Sugarcane (Ukhu)
notes: Real cultivation cycle runs 300-360 days (occasionally more) — durationDays is deliberately set to 365 rather than the literal figure so this app's rotation planner correctly treats it as occupying the land for the better part of a year, the same way it already treats apple orchards, instead of wrongly trying to slot it into a single 4-month season

After the first ('plant crop') harvest, the stubble regrows without replanting for 1-3 more cheaper 'ratoon' cycles (~43% of plant-crop cost) — this listing uses plant-crop economics as the more conservative default for a first-time decision

Nepal has a government-set minimum support price (MSP, since 2018) paid partly by the mill and partly as a direct subsidy — but real news reporting through 2025 documents mills repeatedly paying farmers BELOW the mandated minimum, and multi-year subsidy non-payment disputes. The official MSP is a floor, not a guarantee of what you'll actually be paid

Directly documented as a cause of jute's sharp decline in the eastern Terai — 'jute area has been replaced by sugarcane due to its high yield potential and high profit margin' (peer-reviewed 2013 study) — the two crops compete for the same land and season
Very heavy water demand (~200 tonnes of water per tonne of cane produced) — a real constraint where irrigation access is limited
sources: Zones/districts: Terai-only, no hill/high-hill cultivation found; commercial production (>5,000 ha) concentrated in Mahottari, Sarlahi, Rautahat, Nawalparasi, Kapilbastu — Nepal-sourced (MoALD 2019/2020, cited in Gham Power and ScienceDirect 'The sugarcane industry in Nepal: Opportunities and challenges,' 2016)

Duration: Nepal's own released varieties (Jitpur 1-4, Agriculture and Forestry University Rampur) mature in 300-360 days; full commercial spring-planted cycles run ~13-14 months in practice — Nepal-sourced (Rijal, 'Sugarcane Production in Nepal,' Acta Scientific Agriculture 3(8), 2019). See notes for why this dataset uses 365 instead of the literal figure

Water/soil: heavy irrigation need (furrow method standard), well-drained loam/sandy-loam preferred, workable but sub-optimal on heavy clay — Nepal-sourced (Rijal 2019; a Sunsari/Morang field economics study) corroborated by Bihar's RPCAU Pusa sugarcane research station (India, directly adjacent to the Nepal Terai)

Rotation: Poaceae/grass family (same broad family as rice/wheat/maize/millet — cereals are deliberately excluded from this app's same-family disease-risk penalty, unlike allium/brassica/solanaceae, since cereal-on-cereal rotations like rice-wheat are agronomically sound, not risky). Confirmed heavy nitrogen feeder — Nepal's blanket recommendation is N120:P60:K40 kg/ha — commonly rotated with a legume break crop to restore soil nitrogen, per a peer-reviewed study on legume rotation in sugarcane soils

Cost: NPR 245,912/ha (~NPR 99,500/acre) for a plant-crop cycle; ratoon cycles ~43% of that — Pokharel et al., 'Dynamics and Economic Analysis of Sugarcane Production in Eastern Plains of Nepal,' Current Agricultural Research Journal 7(2), 2019 (80-farmer survey, Sunsari & Morang districts, 2017/18 data). This is a real Sunsari-district figure but is 7-8 years old — Nepal-wide labor and fertilizer cost inflation over that period make current costs very likely substantially higher (plausibly NPR 150,000-200,000+/acre), though no more recent Nepal-specific figure could be confirmed

Yield: 49.67 t/ha (~20 t/acre) national average (MoALD 2019, used here as the conservative default) vs. 62.2 t/ha (~25 t/acre) in the same Sunsari/Morang field study — both Nepal-sourced. Nepal's national yield and sugar-recovery rate both run below India's

Price: NPR 5,850-6,900/tonne, spanning Nepal's government MSP+subsidy system across the 2024/25-2025/26 seasons (mill-only portion at the low end, full MSP+subsidy at the high end) — Nepal-sourced (Kathmandu Post MSP coverage, 2023-2025). The 2025/26 figure itself has a genuine unresolved contradiction in the source reporting (flagged, not resolved by guessing), and real-world underpayment below this mandated range is well documented (see notes) — treat this range as optimistic rather than guaranteed

monthlyCalendar.sourceNote: Treated as a single long-cycle annual (~10-12 months), not a fruiting perennial: a Nepal source gives Falgun-Chaitra (mid-Feb-mid-Apr) as peak harvest/crushing time, so spring planting/tillering (Mar-Apr, using the Indian subtropical spring-planting norm since no Nepal-specific planting month was found) leads into a long cane-growth and sugar-accumulation ('fruit_development') phase before winter harvest.

enterprises.name: Cauliflower (Phulgobi)
notes: Chitwan is Nepal's named cauliflower belt (Inner Terai); hill districts (Tistung, Palung, Daman) grow a real May-September off-season crop specifically to supply Kathmandu/Terai markets when Terai's own supply is out of season

Genuine same-family (Brassica) disease risk with mustard: clubroot has caused severe, documented epidemics in Nepal since 2004, and the same pathogen has established in West Bengal's Terai belt — avoid planting right after mustard on the same land
Price swings are extreme and well-documented — a 2026 supply disruption saw retail prices spike 200% in a single month
Recently reported growing in Mustang's high-altitude villages as warming temperatures make it newly viable there — real but new, not yet a traditional stronghold
sources: Zones/season: Terai/hills main season Sept-Dec (rabi); a genuine second hill-grown kharif crop (May-Sept) fills Terai's off-season gap — Nepal-sourced (Chitwan cauliflower-belt literature; ANSAB/NEAT off-season vegetable value-chain analysis, 2011). High-hills (Mustang) is real but recent/climate-driven, lower confidence — Kathmandu Post, Dec 2024

Cost: NPR 10,147/ropani (~NPR 80,700/acre), Chitwan — District Agriculture Development Office, Bagmati Province, 'Production Cost Analysis of Major Vegetables,' 2019 household survey. Cross-district spread documented in the same study: Makwanpur cheaper (~NPR 75,900/acre), Kathmandu Valley far more expensive (~NPR 222,700/acre)

Yield: 46,497 ha / 696,000 t nationally = 14.97 t/ha (~60.6 quintal/acre) — MoALD 'Statistical Information on Nepalese Agriculture,' FY2080/81 (2023/24). Cross-checked against core Terai districts (Sarlahi 17.5 t/ha, Rupandehi 16.2 t/ha, Kapilvastu 15.5 t/ha) — reasonably consistent with the national figure, unlike tomato (see that entry)

Price: NPR 1,800-12,000/quintal — Kalimati Fruits & Vegetables Market Development Board wholesale rates (Kathmandu, not Terai farm-gate), spanning a documented glut low (~NPR 1,200-1,800/quintal, March 2025) to a documented scarcity-driven spike (~200% increase, Jan-Feb 2026). Genuinely this volatile, not a modeling error

Rotation: Brassica family, same as mustard already in this dataset — clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae) is a confirmed shared pathogen with documented severe Nepal epidemics since 2004 (Makwanpur district) and established presence in West Bengal's Terai belt since the 1980s. Soil-borne spores persist 4-20 years, so a single-season rotation gap is a real but partial mitigation, not a full fix

enterprises.name: Cabbage (Bandagobi)
notes: Same Brassica-family clubroot disease risk as cauliflower and mustard — a documented Nepal case exists specifically for cabbage (Sidhuwa) — avoid planting right after either on the same land
Grown alongside cauliflower in the same Tistung/Palung/Daman hill off-season system, though its own off-season window (Oct-Nov) is narrower than cauliflower's
Cost figure here is genuinely the weakest in this dataset — see sources
sources: Zones/season: Terai winter (rabi) plus a hill-grown off-season window — Nepal-sourced (off-season vegetable value-chain literature, same as cauliflower)

Price: NPR 2,000-6,000/quintal — Kalimati wholesale rates, including a documented ~28% glut-driven crash (Dec 2018) — Kathmandu wholesale, not Terai farm-gate
Rotation: Brassica family — clubroot documented specifically in Nepal cabbage (a Sidhuwa district case study on managing the disease), same pathogen and same risk profile as cauliflower/mustard

enterprises.name: Tomato (Golbheda)
notes: Main cash crop of Mid-Terai in winter; a real off-season (July-October) hill/tunnel crop fills the gap when Terai can't supply

Genuine, THREE independently-documented same-family (Solanaceae) disease risks with potato: bacterial wilt (rotation cuts incidence 64-94% in studies), late blight (volunteer potato tubers left in soil directly seed the next crop), and root-knot nematodes — avoid planting right after potato on the same land
Nepal's most price-volatile vegetable found in this research: documented crashes to NPR 500-1,200/quintal during gluts and spikes above NPR 10,000/quintal during supply gaps, within the same year
Even in a documented GOOD production year, Terai farmers reported getting only NPR 3,000-3,500/quintal at the farm gate — well below Kathmandu wholesale ceiling prices
sources: Zones/season: Terai winter (Nov-March, rabi) as a named Mid-Terai cash crop; off-season (July-Oct, kharif) filled by hill/tunnel production — Nepal-sourced. High-hills (Mustang) newly documented — Kathmandu Post, Dec 2024

Cost: NPR 33,741/ropani (~NPR 268,400/acre), Chitwan open-field — District Agriculture Development Office, Bagmati Province, 'Production Cost Analysis of Major Vegetables,' 2019. A hills/tunnel off-season cross-check (Kaski district) found meaningfully higher cost (~NPR 352,200/acre) consistent with protected cultivation being more capital-intensive — used as context, not the primary figure

Yield: 26,791 ha / 552,607 t nationally = 20.63 t/ha (~83.5 quintal/acre) — MoALD FY2080/81. Flagged explicitly: Terai-specific districts run meaningfully LOWER (Rupandehi 16.3, Kapilvastu 14.7, Mahottari 14.6 t/ha) — the national figure is likely pulled up by high-input hill/tunnel production. Used here since this crop spans Terai/hills/high-hills (matching how potato's multi-zone economics are handled), but a pure-Terai estimate would sit closer to 55-65 quintal/acre

Price: NPR 800-9,000/quintal — Kalimati wholesale plus documented real extremes: a April 2025 glut crash to ~NPR 950/quintal (farmers left produce to rot) and an Oct 2024 supply-gap spike above NPR 10,000/quintal. A rare real farm-gate data point from the same April 2025 reporting: Terai farmers got only NPR 3,000-3,500/quintal even in a good year — confirming a large, genuine wholesale-vs-farm-gate gap

Rotation: Solanaceae family, same as potato already in this dataset (reclassified from a generic 'tuber' label to its actual botanical family specifically to make this connection). Three independently-documented disease mechanisms link potato and tomato: bacterial wilt (Ralstonia solanacearum, 400+ host species, standard advisory is no more than 1-in-3-years Solanaceae), late blight (volunteer potato tubers are a documented primary inoculum source for a following tomato crop), and root-knot nematodes

enterprises.name: Mango (Aap)

enterprises.name: Grape (Angur)
notes: This is the lowest-confidence entry of the batch. The database itself rates it 'marginal' cultivation with 'low' agronomic_suitability -- Nepal's only documented commercial vineyard belt is Dhading (Thakre Rural Municipality), and commercial-scale growing only began in 2016. Included because real, non-trial commercial cultivation genuinely exists (regional_cultivation=1), unlike almond/coconut/date palm, but this is a genuinely marginal/emerging crop, not an established one -- flag accordingly wherever this entry surfaces.

Nepal's monsoon genuinely conflicts with natural grape ripening: harvest would naturally fall in Aug-Sep (peak monsoon), so growers use hydrogen cyanamide to force early budburst and pull harvest forward to Jun-Jul. Both zaid (flowering) and kharif (the ripening/harvest window, forced-early or natural) are marked for this reason -- see season sourcing below.

Nepal's own commercial output is reported as going mostly to juice/wine production rather than fresh table-grape sale, which is part of why the price estimate below leans toward the low end of its India analog rather than above it.

Nepal imports large volumes (Rs 1.54 billion, FY2018/19) -- still import-dependent, not an established belt' (source: The Himalayan Times, 'Commercial grape farming, one of its kind, starts in Dhading'). plant_environment_requirements: temperature 15-40C (general viticulture knowledge, confidence 0.3, not Nepal-cited); soil_ph optimal 6.5-7.5 (general fallback, confidence 0.3); years_to_first_harvest optimal 2-3 years (confidence 0.3, inferred from one farm's account).
Zones: hills only -- the DB's only region with documented real cultivation is Mid-Hills (1000-2000m), which falls inside gram's hills bucket (~300-2000m).

Season: Nepal-specific web research (Table Grape Production in the Subtropics and Prospects for Nepal, horticulturenepal.org; Kathmandu Post coverage of Nepali vineyards) confirms flowering Apr-early May and a ~4-5 month berry maturation period, putting natural harvest in Aug-Sep -- squarely inside the monsoon, which multiple sources explicitly flag as Nepal viticulture's central agronomic problem (berry splitting/disease pressure). Growers apply hydrogen cyanamide to force budburst earlier and pull the harvest window to Jun-Jul to beat the monsoon. zaid (flowering) + kharif (ripening/harvest, whichever timing) are both marked, mirroring gram's existing litchi entry's precedent of marking both seasons when harvest genuinely straddles that boundary rather than forcing a single season. rabi (winter dormancy) is omitted since nothing about the vine's active cycle happens then, matching gram's existing kiwi entry's precedent of being selective for a vine/perennial rather than defaulting to all three seasons.

Cost: NPR 150,000/acre/year (established vineyard) -- ESTIMATE, low confidence, India-analog fallback (no Nepal-specific figure was found). An India (Sangli district, Maharashtra) grape-economics study gives an annual maintenance-stage cost of INR 42,000-44,000/acre for its 3-10yr and >15yr production stages (~NPR 67,000-70,000/acre at the fixed 1 INR = NPR 1.6 peg); the same study's fuller 'cost of cultivation' figure was INR 267,669/acre (~NPR 428,000/acre). NPR 150,000/acre was chosen between these two anchors: above the bare maintenance-only figure to reflect Nepal's added monsoon disease-management burden (a documented real problem here, unlike Maharashtra's dry-season ripening) and recurring trellis/support-structure upkeep -- a real cost specific to grape among this batch's crops -- but below the full Maharashtra commercial-intensity figure since Nepal's operation is smaller-scale and less input-intensive. This is the least-grounded cost figure in this entry; treat as a rough bracket, not a verified number.

Yield: 60 quintal/acre -- ESTIMATE, medium-low confidence. A Nepal-specific source (horticulturenepal.org, via search) states well-cared vines yield ~20 MT/ha (range 15-35 MT/ha), i.e. ~81 quintal/acre at the average and ~61-142 quintal/acre across the range (1 ha = 2.471 acre). 60 quintal/acre was chosen near the low end of that range rather than the ~81 quintal/acre average, because the same research also turned up explicit statements that Nepal's actual berry yield and quality are 'still poor,' limiting commercial scale-up (Himalayan Times) -- the optimistic 'well cared' average was judged too generous for a crop the database itself rates 'marginal'/'low suitability.'

Price: NPR 5,000-7,000/quintal (NPR 50-70/kg) farm-gate -- ESTIMATE, low confidence, India-analog fallback. The same India (Sangli) study's own gross-return/yield figures imply a farm-gate price of ~INR 40/kg (~NPR 64/kg at the 1.6 peg) for a mature, quality-consistent commercial table-grape vineyard; this was used as the central anchor since it is already a farm-gate (not wholesale/retail) figure, unlike some other sources found. Kalimati wholesale/retail grape prices also seen during research (NPR 140-230/kg for green/black grapes) were deliberately NOT used, since that produce is imported table grape, not Nepal-grown, and is a poor proxy for local farm-gate value -- consistent with this project's known pattern of retail/wholesale prices overstating true farm-gate by a wide margin.
