Sanity check: implied B:C = 60 x avg(5000,7000) / 150000 = 2.4, comparable to rice (~2.1) and well inside this app's 1.5-5 sanity band -- but given how many of this entry's individual inputs are India-analog estimates rather than Nepal citations, this B:C should be read as 'plausible order of magnitude,' not a verified figure.

enterprises.name: Lemon (Nimbu)
notes: Distinct from gram's existing 'lime' entry (Citrus aurantifolia/Kagati) -- this is true lemon, Citrus limon/Nimbu. Nepal's own database treats it as an 'underutilized,' scattered dooryard/minor crop, not commercially zoned or separately tracked in official statistics -- weaker commercial standing than lime, so numbers here are more conservative than lime's.

~90% of Nepal's urban lemon demand is currently met by imports from India per a Nepal-focused news profile -- a real import-substitution gap, though today's typical grower is small-scale/rainfed on marginal land with limited management, not the exceptional commercial Chitwan grower featured in that same article.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plant_id 53). regional_crops: Terai (marginal, 'scattered Terai through Mid-Hills, dooryard/minor crop... classified as underutilized, not commercially zoned') and Mid-Hills (marginal, 'low to high-hills range'), both citing Thapa/Gotame/Dhimal 2021, Nepal Horticulture Society -- a real academic source, cultivation_status is 'marginal' not 'not_found'. Env requirements (temp 13-37C, rainfall 1000-2000mm, soil pH 5.5-6.5 optimal) are flagged in the DB itself as general citrus fallback, not Nepal-specific (confidence 0.3).
Zones: Terai (60-300m) + Mid-Hills (1000-2000m, mapped to gram's 'hills' band) per the two regional_crops rows above.

Season: no direct Nepal lemon harvest-calendar source found in this quick pass; defaulted to all three seasons (matches this app's existing 'lime' entry, a closely related citrus with similar multi-flush fruiting habit in Nepal's climate) rather than forcing a single season without evidence.

Cost: WEB, moderate confidence. A Nepal news profile (OnlineKhabar, Chitwan commercial grower) cites NPR 150,000-200,000/acre annual maintenance after year 2, but that grower is an atypical intensive commercial outlier (the article's own news hook). Discounted toward NPR 100,000/acre to better represent the DB's own 'marginal land, poor management' typical-grower framing.

Yield: WEB, low-moderate confidence. Nepal research cites a 147 kg/tree/year MAXIMUM, explicitly caveated that most orchards are rainfed/marginal with poor management and yield less. Used ~35 quintal/acre, in line with this app's own already-vetted 'lime' entry (33.67 quintal/acre, real MRSMP Palpa data) given the two citrus share similar underutilized status.

Price: WEB, moderate confidence. Chitwan vegetable-market retail was NPR 100-200/kg; discounted ~55-60% toward farm-gate (NPR 6,000-9,000/quintal) per this project's standing finding that retail/local-market prices run 2-4x farm-gate. Implied B:C ~2.6, similar order to rice/potato.

enterprises.name: Muskmelon (Kharbuja)
notes: LOWEST-CONFIDENCE agronomic citation of this batch: the DB's own region-suitability note calls this 'the weakest-data crop of this batch: not_found for Nepal specifics,' with Terai suitability estimated purely by analogy to watermelon ('inference, not a citation'). Included anyway because muskmelon/kharbuja is a real, well-known Terai riverbed summer melon (confirmed by general agricultural knowledge and cross-checked against India cultivation data), not a fabrication -- but flagged here as the entry with the weakest direct sourcing.

Economics deliberately mirrored close to this app's own existing 'watermelon' entry, since the DB explicitly treats muskmelon as agronomically near-identical to watermelon (same Terai/Inner-Terai riverbed style, often intercropped) -- an internally consistent way to estimate a crop this under-cited.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plant_id 58). regional_crops: Terai (marginal, by explicit analogy to watermelon -- see confidence caveat in notes). Env requirements (temp 24-32C optimal/max, soil pH 6.0-7.0) also flagged in the DB as 'general cucurbit fallback by analogy to watermelon, not Nepal-sourced at all' (confidence 0.2).
Zones: Terai (60-300m) only, matching the one regional_crops row and watermelon's own real growing-district footprint (Bardiya/Banke/Parsa/Bara/Rautahat/Chitwan).

Season: WEB. India sources (plains regions) place sowing Oct-Mar (mid-Feb ideal) or Feb-Apr, with harvest 80-110 days later. This matches this app's own 'watermelon' entry (Feb sow / May harvest, zaid). No Nepal-specific muskmelon calendar was found in this quick pass, so zaid timing is inferred from the same riverbed-melon pattern as watermelon plus general India sowing-window data. Duration set to 90 days (mid-point of the 80-110 day range found).

Cost: WEB, low-moderate confidence -- no direct Nepal figure found. Set at NPR 80,000/acre by analogy to this app's own vetted 'watermelon' entry (NPR 95,000/acre), slightly reduced since muskmelon needs marginally less intensive management per India sources.

Yield: WEB (India). Commercial India yields range widely by variety: Hara Madhu ~50 quintal/acre, MH-27/MH-51 ~88-89 quintal/acre, general estimates 80-120+ quintal/acre with hybrids. Used a moderate 65 quintal/acre, below India's optimized-hybrid range to reflect likely less-intensive Nepal smallholder practice.

Price: WEB (India mandi, converted/discounted). India mandi average ~Rs 3,312/quintal (range Rs 1,500-7,000; peak-glut wholesale Rs 1,800-2,500/quintal). Converted toward NPR and discounted slightly toward farm-gate, then anchored close to this app's own watermelon price band (NPR 2,700-3,500/quintal) as the closer, already-vetted Nepal proxy. Implied B:C ~2.8, close to watermelon's own ~2.6.

enterprises.name: Peach (Aaru)
notes: Well-grounded agronomically: real named growing locations (Marpha/Mustang, Jumla in the high-hills; 'extensively grown' 1000-2800m in mid-hills) from an FAO Nepal deciduous-fruit report, the same source class already backing this app's apple/mango entries.

Same climate niche as this app's existing 'apple' entry (high-hills, Mustang) -- economics were sanity-checked against apple's numbers (NPR 91,000/acre cost, 35 quintal/acre yield) for plausibility given no equally strong Nepal-specific peach cost/price citation was found.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plant_id 117), source: FAO Deciduous Fruit Production in Nepal. regional_crops: Mid-Hills (cultivated, 'extensively grown 1000-2800m') and High Hills (cultivated, 'Marpha/Mustang, Jumla'). Also has a years_to_first_harvest row (2-4 years optimal, confidence 0.4, flagged as a general Nepal fruit-crop statement not peach-specific).
Zones: Mid-Hills + High Hills per the two cultivated-status regional_crops rows -> gram's 'hills' + 'high-hills'.
Season: no dedicated Nepal peach phenology source found; defaulted to all three seasons as a perennial orchard tree, matching this app's existing apple/mango/litchi/lime convention.

Soil/water: no DB soil_ph row exists for peach; used general stone-fruit knowledge (well-drained loamy soil) and mirrored apple's own soil/water tags (loamy, sandy-loam; rainfed+irrigated) given the same high-hills/mid-hills orchard context, including Mustang's irrigation-dependent arid climate.

Cost: WEB, moderate confidence. A general search attributed NPR 100,000-200,000/acre annual maintenance to Nepal peach orchards, though the framing may partly blend with generic fruit-orchard figures. Used NPR 110,000/acre, close to apple's own vetted NPR 91,000/acre for the same climate zone.
Yield: WEB (blended Nepal/general). 30-40 kg/tree/year cited, equivalent to ~8-12 tonnes/ha (~32-49 quintal/acre). Used 40 quintal/acre, in line with apple (35) and mango (44) in this dataset.

Price: WEB, low-moderate confidence -- no direct Nepal peach farm-gate figure found; Kathmandu retail listings (out-of-stock indicative price ~NPR 299/kg) were discounted ~55-60% toward farm-gate (NPR 9,000-13,000/quintal), similar order to mango/litchi. Implied B:C ~4.0.

enterprises.name: Persimmon (Haluwabed)
notes: LOWEST-CONFIDENCE ECONOMICS of this batch, flagged clearly: no Nepal cost, yield, or farm-gate price citation was found anywhere in this quick pass. Only a single Mid-Hills (Kathmandu valley) cultivation citation exists agronomically, and it explicitly frames persimmon as a tourism/export-oriented niche crop -- i.e. a thin, poorly-tracked market, not a mainstream commodity like mango or litchi.

Retail/wholesale price sources found (NPR ~810-980/kg retail Kathmandu/Pokhara; ~$4.2-5.2/kg wholesale) were suspiciously high and precise, and are treated with real skepticism here -- discounted substantially toward a still-premium-but-more-plausible farm-gate estimate (NPR 12,000-18,000/quintal) rather than used directly, since taking them at face value would have produced a B:C ratio far outside this app's realistic 1.5-5 band.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plant_id 121), source: FAO Deciduous Fruit Production in Nepal. regional_crops: Mid-Hills only (cultivated, 'Kathmandu, Bhaktapur, Lalitpur -- FAO describes broader warm temperate areas suitability too'). Also a years_to_first_harvest row (3-5 years optimal, confidence 0.3, flagged as 'estimate, not Nepal-sourced').

Zones: Mid-Hills only (1000-2000m) -> gram's 'hills'. No high-hills evidence was found in the DB, so high-hills was NOT added despite FAO's vaguer 'warm temperate areas' language -- kept to the one directly-evidenced zone.
Season: no Nepal persimmon harvest-calendar source found; defaulted to all three seasons as a perennial orchard tree (same convention as apple/mango/litchi/lime).

Soil/water: no DB soil_ph row exists for persimmon; used general horticultural knowledge (persimmon tolerates a wider soil range, including heavier clay, better than most fruit trees; deep well-drained loam preferred) and mirrored the Kathmandu-valley orchard water pattern (rainfed + supplemental irrigation) used elsewhere in this dataset.

Cost: NOT researched with a direct citation -- NPR 100,000/acre is this app's own estimate, set by analogy to peach/apple's established-orchard maintenance cost in a comparable mid-hills climate. LOW CONFIDENCE.

Yield: NOT researched with a direct citation -- 30 quintal/acre is a conservative general persimmon-orchard estimate (world/India ranges run ~32-61 quintal/acre for mature orchards); set low given Nepal cultivation is mostly non-intensive/dooryard-style even where 'cultivated'. LOW CONFIDENCE.

Price: WEB, LOW CONFIDENCE -- see notes above on the retail/wholesale figures found and why they were discounted rather than used directly. NPR 12,000-18,000/quintal is a deliberately conservative estimate; implied B:C ~4.5, at the upper edge of this app's realistic 1.5-5 band, consistent with treating this as a genuine high-value niche fruit rather than a data error.

enterprises.name: Plum (Aaru Bakhada)
notes: Agronomics are real but derived entirely BY ANALOGY to peach in the source database itself ('grown wherever peach is grown except early-spring-frost areas, 1000-2800m' / 'same range as peach') -- same underlying FAO report, not an independent plum-specific citation. Zones/season/soil/water here follow that same peach analogy.

Economics also have no direct Nepal citation; set slightly below peach's own estimate (smaller trees, generally lower per-tree yield in the general sources found) rather than fabricating an independent figure.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plant_id 118), source: FAO Deciduous Fruit Production in Nepal. regional_crops: Mid-Hills (cultivated, 'grown wherever peach is grown except early-spring-frost areas, 1000-2800m') and High Hills (cultivated, 'same range as peach') -- both explicitly by-analogy-to-peach in the source's own notes, confidence 0.6 on the elevation row.
Zones: Mid-Hills + High Hills per the two regional_crops rows -> gram's 'hills' + 'high-hills', matching peach.
Season: no dedicated Nepal plum phenology source found; defaulted to all three seasons as a perennial orchard tree, matching apple/mango/litchi/lime/peach.

Soil: WEB (general/India). One India source cites red lateritic soil, pH 5.8-6.2, good drainage; generalized to loamy/sandy-loam well-drained soil tags consistent with peach's own entry in this batch.

Cost: NOT directly researched for Nepal -- NPR 90,000/acre is this app's own estimate, set slightly below peach's NPR 110,000/acre (smaller tree, comparable but somewhat lighter management). LOW-MODERATE CONFIDENCE.

Yield: WEB (general, not Nepal-specific). 25-30 kg/tree/year cited; converted toward ~35 quintal/acre using an assumed plum-orchard tree density, kept close to peach's 40 quintal/acre given the DB's own 'grown wherever peach is grown' framing.

Price: NOT directly researched for Nepal -- no clean per-kg plum figure was retrievable (only a per-piece retail listing, not usable). NPR 8,000-11,000/quintal is estimated slightly below peach's price band. Implied B:C ~3.7. LOW-MODERATE CONFIDENCE -- weakest-sourced economics after persimmon.

enterprises.name: Cassava (Ghar Tarul)
notes: Named 'Cassava (Ghar Tarul)' rather than plain 'Tarul' to avoid collision/confusion with this app's existing 'Yam (Tarul)' entry -- Nepali sources use 'Ghar Tarul' or 'Simal Tarul' specifically for cassava (Manihot esculenta) as distinct from true yam (Dioscorea spp.).

Real, solid Terai cultivation evidence (~30 years grown, MoALD bundles it into an 'Others' root/tuber category so it's not separately tracked in national statistics) plus an explicit note that Inner Terai has 'massive cultivation potential... flagged for expansion' -- a genuine, if currently under-the-radar, crop.

Nepal retail price found (NPR ~270-420/kg on a Kathmandu specialty-grocery delivery site) looks like novelty/boutique urban pricing, not representative of a bulk Terai staple root crop -- discounted heavily in favor of an India (Kerala/Tamil Nadu) mandi-price analog instead, which is far more consistent with cassava's usual role as a cheap staple/starch crop.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plant_id 42), source: 'Status and Prospects of Root and Tuber Crops in Nepal' (Nepal Horticulture Society, citing MoALD 2019). regional_crops: Terai (cultivated, high agronomic suitability, '~30 years, low-input traditional techniques, no organized breeding program') and Inner Terai (marginal, low agronomic suitability, explicitly flagged for expansion: 'massive cultivation of tapioca in Siwalik and Inner Terai'). Env requirements: temperature 12-40C (optimal 25-30C), rainfall 500-5000mm (drought-tolerant), soil pH 5.5-8.0 (wide tolerance) -- confidence 0.4, labeled 'regional fallback'.

Zones: Terai + Inner Terai both fold into gram's single 'terai' zone tag (no separate 'inner-terai' category exists in this schema) -- same convention already used for this app's 'watermelon' entry, whose real growing districts include Inner Terai areas like Chitwan/Makwanpur under a terai-only zone tag.

Season: WEB (India analog, Kerala/Tamil Nadu -- the best-documented South Asian cassava belt). Rainfed planting is done pre-monsoon/monsoon-onset (April-May in Kerala; April cited generally for rainfed crops), harvested 8-12 months later. Tagged 'kharif' only (planting-season convention), matching this app's own 'yam' and 'taro' entries, which are also long-duration root crops tagged with a single planting season despite spanning most of the year.

Duration: WEB. Most sources cite 8-12 months to harvest (commonly '9-11 months', up to 11-12 for full maturity). Set to 270 days (9 months), within the requested 240-300 day range and matching yam's own 270-day precedent in this dataset.

Soil/water: sandy-loam/loamy/alluvial soil (matches yam's own soil tags for a Terai/hills root crop; cassava specifically needs good drainage and dislikes waterlogging, consistent with excluding heavy clay). Water set to rainfed-only, matching yam's own treatment and cassava's well-known status as a classic low-input, drought-tolerant subsistence/famine-reserve root crop (also consistent with the DB's own 500-5000mm wide rainfall tolerance).

Cost: WEB (India analog, Kerala), moderate confidence, explicitly flagged as India not Nepal. Kerala cost of cultivation ~INR 150,000-200,000/ha (~NPR 97,000-129,000/acre after conversion) for intensive input use; roughly halved to NPR 55,000/acre to reflect Nepal's own DB-documented 'low-input, traditional' cultivation style rather than Kerala's more intensive practice.

Yield: WEB (India analog), moderate confidence. Kerala state average is a very high 41.77 tonnes/ha (~169 quintal/acre, intensive/improved varieties); other general sources cite 10-15 tonnes/acre (~100-150 quintal/acre) or 'typical' 80 quintal/acre. Used a conservative 90 quintal/acre given Nepal's low-input traditional practice, well below Kerala's optimized state average.

Price: WEB (India analog, Kerala/Tamil Nadu mandi), moderate confidence, explicitly flagged as India not Nepal -- Nepal's own retail figure was rejected as unrepresentative (see notes). India mandi ~INR 3,200/quintal, Kerala retail ~INR 4,000/quintal-equivalent; used NPR 2,000-3,000/quintal, which also lines up closely with this app's own already-vetted 'yam' and 'taro' entries (NPR 2,500-4,000/quintal) for comparable Nepal staple root crops. Implied B:C ~4.1.

enterprises.name: Amaranth (Lunde Saag)
notes: Two distinct forms exist in Nepal: a fast-growing leafy saag (latte/lunde) common in the Terai, and a separate grain type (chaulai/marsi) grown as a traditional high-altitude food-security crop in Dolakha/Jumla. This entry models the far more common leafy-vegetable form, not the grain crop -- grain amaranth trades in a completely different specialty/export market (~$2.70-8.73/kg globally) that would badly mismatch this entry's economics if used.

Hills (mid-hills) inclusion is general-knowledge inference -- amaranth saag is a ubiquitous Nepali kitchen-garden green across elevation bands -- since the database's own regional_crops rows only directly document Terai (leafy) and Mountain/high-hills (grain) endpoints, not Mid-Hills specifically.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plant_id 66). regional_crops/plant_region_suitability confirm Terai (leafy type, 'fast-growing Terai vegetable', high agronomic suitability) and Mountain (grain type/chaulai, Dolakha & Jumla, NARC-linked multi-year stability trials 2018-2020, high agronomic suitability), both citing MDPI Agriculture 'Underutilized Grain Crops in Western Mountains of Nepal.' No plant_environment_requirements (temperature/rainfall/soil_ph) rows were present for this crop in the database.

Season: WEB (not Nepal-specific). Best growing windows given as summer (Feb-Apr) and rainy season (Jun-Jul), avoiding peak winter/May; mapped to zaid + kharif. Duration: 50-60 days to first harvest of tender greens, with multiple cuttings possible every 7-10 days through ~60 days -- consistent across several general growing guides.

Cost: WEB, medium confidence, real Nepal source but not amaranth-specific. Department of Agriculture, Bagmati Province 'Production Cost Analysis of Major Vegetables' leafy-vegetable-basket figures (the same underlying source category already used for this file's spinach entry) -- Chitwan NPR 6,791.66/ropani, converted at 7.955 ropani/acre = ~NPR 54,000/acre. Used the Chitwan (Terai-adjacent, lower-cost) figure rather than the same study's much higher Kathmandu figure (NPR 15,500/ropani, ~NPR 123,000/acre) since Terai is amaranth's primary documented zone.

Yield: WEB, medium-high confidence -- two independently converging estimates. A Nepal-specific figure of 20-30 t/ha (~81-121 quintal/acre) and an independent India figure of 10 t/acre (100 quintal/acre) land in the same range. This entry uses 100 quintal/acre.

Price: WEB, low-medium confidence, analogy-based. NOT found Nepal-specific for amaranth/saag despite a dedicated Kalimati search (only generic market-tracker homepages surfaced, no crop-specific figure). Proxied from this file's own already-corrected spinach entry (NPR 1,500-2,500/quintal, a bulk-wholesale leafy-green farm-gate estimate), nudged slightly lower (1,500-2,200) since amaranth saag is typically a cheaper, more everyday green than spinach in Nepal markets; loosely cross-checked against an India retail figure of Rs 11/kg (~NPR 1,760/quintal via the fixed NPR:INR peg), which lands inside this range.
Implied B:C ratio ~3.4 at these figures -- plausible for a fast multi-cut leafy green, in the same range as this file's well-grounded crops.

enterprises.name: Ash Gourd (Kubhindo)
notes: LOWEST-CONFIDENCE economics in this batch alongside sweet_corn: both cost and price are this app's own analogy-based estimates, not direct citations -- no Nepal or India source with a matching cost/price figure was found despite two dedicated search passes.

Thick-rinded, long-storage gourd (also called winter melon/white gourd) -- traditionally kept for months after harvest (dried 'sukeko kubhindo' preparations), which likely dampens its price volatility relative to more perishable gourds, hence the lower priceVolatility score here.

Hills inclusion is general-knowledge inference (kubhindo is commonly grown in Nepali hill kitchen gardens, often trained over roofs/fences) -- the database's regional_crops evidence only directly documents Terai (Rupandehi survey).

One India source claimed a yield of '240 quintals per acre' -- almost certainly a mislabeled per-HECTARE figure (240 quintal/ha = 24 t/ha matches the well-corroborated Indu-variety figure below almost exactly, while 240 quintal/ACRE would be wildly out of line with every other source). Excluded to avoid exactly the kind of dropped-zero/wrong-unit bug this project has repeatedly had to fix.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plant_id 113). regional_crops/plant_region_suitability confirm Terai cultivation ('part of the Terai summer vegetable list', Rupandehi district survey, high agronomic suitability), citing the JICA Vegetable Farming Techniques Manual (District Agriculture Development Office). No Mid/High-Hill rows present in the database for this crop, and no plant_environment_requirements rows.

Season: WEB. One source states Nepal sowing windows of Jan-Mar and Sep-Dec (source quality unclear); a clearer north-India source gives Feb-Mar and Jun-Jul. Mapped the clearer Feb-Mar/Jun-Jul pattern to zaid + kharif, consistent with this file's other gourds.

Duration: WEB. 90-150 days depending on source; one figure states 145 days from planting to harvest with a 2kg/acre seed rate. This entry uses 140 days, on the long end, consistent with ash gourd's role as a longer-season storage crop rather than a quick-turnover vegetable.

Yield: WEB, medium confidence. General range 10-35 t/ha across sources, with an Indu-variety figure of 24.5 t/ha as the most specific single citation. A 70-75 t/ha claim for one unnamed variety is treated as an unrepresentative hybrid outlier and not used. This entry uses 100 quintal/acre (~24.7 t/ha), matching the Indu-variety figure closely.

Cost: WEB, LOW CONFIDENCE, estimate not citation. NOT found Nepal- or India-specific despite two dedicated search passes. NPR 60,000/acre is this app's own estimate, set by analogy to this file's existing pumpkin entry (NPR 50,000/acre, a similarly bulky low-input vining cucurbit with comparable yield), nudged up slightly for ash gourd's longer season.

Price: WEB, LOW CONFIDENCE, estimate not citation. NOT found Nepal-specific despite a dedicated Kalimati search (no crop-specific figure surfaced). NPR 2,000-3,000/quintal is this app's own estimate, set by analogy to this file's pumpkin entry (a similarly bulky, low-value-density gourd) rather than to the higher-value fresh gourds (bottle/bitter gourd) already in this file.

Implied B:C ratio ~4.2 at these figures -- within this file's plausible range, but built on two analogy-based (not directly sourced) legs, so treat this entry's economics as the roughest of this batch.

enterprises.name: Ridge Gourd (Pate Ghiraula)
notes: Nepal's own database explicitly notes ridge gourd is 'often lumped with sponge gourd under the shared local name Ghiraula' -- Kalimati market listings and price reports may not always cleanly distinguish the two, so this entry's price should be read as a ridge/sponge-gourd-family estimate rather than a ridge-gourd-only figure (see sponge_gourd, which shares the same price band for this reason).
Requires trellising like this file's existing bottle_gourd entry -- cost estimate reflects that shared infrastructure need.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plant_id 110). regional_crops/plant_region_suitability confirm Terai cultivation ('household/trellis staple', high agronomic suitability), citing the JICA Vegetable Farming Techniques Manual. No Mid/High-Hill rows present in the database, and no plant_environment_requirements rows.
Season: WEB (krishijagran, tractorkarvan, India). 'Summer crop sown Feb-March, monsoon crop sown June-July' consistently reported; mapped to zaid + kharif.

Duration: WEB. Fruit ready 70-80 days after sowing per most sources (one states ~60 days for first harvest, another 120-135 days for full-season yield accumulation). This entry uses 90 days as a middle estimate covering first-harvest-to-tail-end-of-picking.

Yield: WEB (India), medium-high confidence -- two independent, converging figures: a direct '100-125 quintal/acre' claim and a separate '24-26 tonnes/hectare' claim (~97-105 quintal/acre once converted) landing in the same range. This entry uses 100 quintal/acre, the conservative end.

Cost: WEB, LOW CONFIDENCE, estimate not citation. NOT found as a direct per-area rupee figure in this pass (only a vague '₹2.5 lakh profit' marketing claim and an 'organic net income ₹50,000-90,000/acre' range, neither with a matching cost breakdown). NPR 100,000/acre is this app's own estimate, scaled between this file's existing bottle_gourd (NPR 170,000/acre, similar trellis infrastructure, higher yield) and bitter_gourd (NPR 50,000/acre) cost estimates.

Price: WEB, low-medium confidence. Kalimati ghiraula wholesale quotes ranged Rs 40-85/kg across several reports of varying age/reliability (Rs 10/kg and Rs 30/kg reports also appeared, likely reflecting genuine large seasonal swings). Per this task's guidance that raw Kalimati wholesale tends to overstate real farm-gate price, this entry discounts to NPR 3,500-4,500/quintal (~Rs 35-45/kg) rather than using the raw quotes directly.

enterprises.name: Snake Gourd (Chichindo)
notes: The only one of the 4 gourds in this batch where the database positively found NO Mid/High-Hill evidence (rather than simply not mentioning it) -- zones kept strictly to Terai on that basis, unlike its sibling gourds.

sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plant_id 112). regional_crops/plant_region_suitability confirm Terai cultivation only ('confirmed Terai summer vegetable, Rupandehi district survey; no Mid/High-Hill evidence found', high agronomic suitability), citing the JICA Vegetable Farming Techniques Manual. No plant_environment_requirements rows present.

Season: WEB. Rainy-season (Jun-Jul) sowing most consistently cited across India sources, with a broader Feb-Jul window also mentioned; no Nepal-specific sowing month found. Mapped to kharif (primary) + zaid (secondary, from the broader window).
Duration: WEB. ~75 days per one source, general guides cluster 70-90 days. This entry uses 90 days.

Yield: WEB (India), medium confidence. Wide range -- 10-18 t/ha 'average production' cited most consistently, with hybrid/trellis-trained variants reaching 25-50 t/ha. This entry uses the conservative average end: 65 quintal/acre (~16 t/ha).

Price: WEB, low-medium confidence. Kalimati chichindo wholesale quotes clustered around Rs 28-30/kg across several recent reports, with one Rs 100/kg outlier. This entry uses NPR 3,000-4,000/quintal (~Rs 30-40/kg), close to the typical cluster.

Implied B:C ratio ~2.5 at these figures -- lands close to the (unreliable) Konkan study's own stated ratio of 1.51 despite this entry deliberately NOT reusing that study's internally-inconsistent raw rupee figures, which is a reassuring independent cross-check.

enterprises.name: Sponge Gourd (Ghiraula)
notes: The best-evidenced of the 4 gourds in this batch: real plant_environment_requirements soil_ph data (6.0-7.0) AND a genuine two-zone regional_crops finding (Terai confirmed staple across 6 named districts; Mid-Hills marginal but present).
See ridge_gourd's notes on the shared 'Ghiraula' naming ambiguity in Nepali markets -- this entry's price should be read as a ridge/sponge-gourd-family estimate.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plant_id 111). regional_crops/plant_region_suitability confirm Terai as a confirmed summer-season staple (Sarlahi, Mahottari, Bara, Parsa, Kaski, Kailali; high agronomic suitability) and Mid-Hills as marginal-but-present ('JICA manual shows season windows here too, suggesting broader adaptability'; low agronomic suitability, regional_cultivation=1), both citing the JICA Vegetable Farming Techniques Manual. plant_environment_requirements gives soil_ph optimal range 6.0-7.0 (general fallback, confidence 0.4).
Season: WEB. Sown twice yearly, mid-Feb to March and mid-May to July, plus general summer availability April-September; mapped to zaid (Feb-Mar) + kharif (May-Jul).
Duration: WEB. 100-120 days to maturity per one source. This entry uses 100 days.

Yield: WEB, medium confidence. One source states 160-200 quintal/hectare (=16-20 t/ha), another states 10-13 t/ha -- overlapping at the low end of the first range. This entry uses 70 quintal/acre (~17.3 t/ha), inside both cited ranges.

Cost: WEB, LOW CONFIDENCE, estimate not citation. NOT found Nepal- or India-specific despite a dedicated search. NPR 90,000/acre is this app's own estimate, matched to this batch's ridge_gourd/snake_gourd cost band (same trellis-cucurbit input profile).

Price: WEB, low-medium confidence. Kalimati ghiraula wholesale quoted at Rs 60/kg (2026) and Rs 85/kg (2019, stale). This entry discounts to NPR 3,500-4,500/quintal (~Rs 35-45/kg) per this task's farm-gate-vs-wholesale guidance, matching ridge_gourd's price given the shared local naming.
Implied B:C ratio ~3.1 at these figures -- comfortably within this file's plausible range.

enterprises.name: Sweet Corn (Mitho Makai)
notes: SINGLE LOWEST-CONFIDENCE entry in this batch -- the source database itself flags sweet corn as its 'weakest-documented crop in this batch: no Nepal source distinguishes sweet corn from field maize regionally,' describing its Nepal presence as a likely-but-unconfirmed peri-urban fresh-market niche (Kathmandu Valley/Kavre/Chitwan), not a well-established crop.

Kept to kharif only (unlike this file's existing maize entry, which has kharif+rabi) -- a secondary spring/rabi planting is plausible by analogy to field maize but was not directly confirmed for SWEET corn specifically in this pass's searches, so this entry deliberately does not assume it.
Zones (terai+hills) follow directly from the database's own 'Kathmandu Valley/Kavre/Chitwan' peri-urban framing -- Kathmandu Valley and Kavre are Mid-Hills, Chitwan is Terai-adjacent.

All cost/yield/price figures are pulled from a single matched India (Haryana) study rather than mixed from several sources, specifically to avoid the cross-source unit-mixing errors this project has repeatedly had to fix.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plant_id 69). regional_crops/plant_region_suitability record Terai cultivation as 'marginal' with low agronomic suitability, citing Kalimati wholesale price reports (via Ratopati) as the only supporting source, plus a note that Nepal sweet corn exports were negligible (5 tonnes, 2022). plant_environment_requirements gives one temperature row (optimal_low 18C, maximum 27C, general fallback, confidence 0.3).

Season: WEB. General Nepal maize-family planting given as May-June (Nepali month Jesta) with July-August harvest; a separate Kathmandu-specific source gives an Aug direct-seeding date (likely a succession/second planting rather than the main window). Mapped to kharif.

Duration: WEB (India). 70-80 days seeding-to-harvest per an India cost study (Sonepat, Haryana) -- notably shorter than this file's existing field-maize entry (100 days), consistent with sweet corn being picked fresh rather than grown to dry-grain maturity. This entry uses 80 days.

Cost/Yield/Price: WEB (India), single matched triplet from 'An Economic Analysis of Sweet Corn Cultivation in Sonepat District of Haryana' -- cost Rs 53,731.52/acre, yield 64.13 quintal/acre, gross return Rs 99,466.61/acre, net return Rs 45,735.08/acre (implied B:C ~1.85). Converted to NPR using the fixed NPR:INR currency peg (1 INR = 1.6 NPR): cost ~NPR 86,000/acre. Price was backed out from this SAME study's own gross return divided by its own yield (not imported from a separate Kalimati/retail source, to keep cost/yield/price internally consistent), then rounded to a NPR 1,800-2,600/quintal range. A Nepal RETAIL figure of ~NPR 141/kg (~14,100/quintal) was also found and explicitly NOT used -- an order of magnitude too high to be a farm-gate figure, exactly the retail-vs-farm-gate trap this task warned about.

Implied B:C ratio ~1.6 at these figures -- deliberately kept close to the source study's own internally-consistent ~1.85, at the lower end of this file's plausible range, appropriate given this is this batch's least-grounded crop.

enterprises.name: Turnip (Salgam)
notes: One of Nepal's original 'temperate vegetables' in the Kathmandu Valley since the mid-19th century, per the cited Nepal Horticulture Society source -- NARC zoning names it a priority crop at Khumaltar, Rukum, and Dadeldhura specifically, and the same source explicitly states it is NOT listed at Terai or High-Hill stations, so zones are kept strictly to hills (the best-evidenced zone call in this batch).
Two distinct sowing windows exist (Asiatic type ~Jul-Sep, temperate/European type ~Oct-Dec) -- both included since Nepal's hill turnip tradition draws on both types depending on variety.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plant_id 63). regional_crops/plant_region_suitability confirm Mid-Hills cultivation only ('one of the original temperate vegetables in Kathmandu Valley since mid-19th century... NARC zoning names it priority crop at Khumaltar, Rukum, Dadeldhura -- not listed at Terai/High-Hill stations', high agronomic suitability), citing Pandey, I.R. & Shakya, S.M. 2016, 'Vegetable Development in the Last Six Decades in Nepal,' Nepal Horticulture Society. No plant_environment_requirements rows present.
Season: WEB. Asiatic-type turnip sown Jul-Sep (explicitly stated as the hill-region window), temperate/European type Oct-Dec in the plains. Mapped to kharif (Jul-Sep) + rabi (Oct-Dec).

Duration: WEB. One India source gives a fast 55-day cycle for a specific variety/yield claim; general guides span 40-90 days depending on Asiatic vs. European type. This entry uses 70 days as a middle estimate.

Yield: WEB (India), medium-high confidence -- converging figures: a direct '105 quintal/acre in 55 days' claim, and a separate '250-400 quintal/hectare' range (~101-162 quintal/acre once converted) that brackets it closely. This entry uses 105 quintal/acre.

Cost: WEB, LOW CONFIDENCE, estimate not citation. NOT found as a clean per-area rupee figure (only a Rs 43,000 'earning' claim tied to the 105 quintal/acre yield figure above, ambiguous whether gross or net). NPR 100,000/acre is this app's own estimate, set below this file's existing radish entry (NPR 221,944/acre, a real but unusually high sourced figure for a related root vegetable) rather than matching it, since no comparably strong Nepal citation exists for turnip specifically.

Price: WEB, low-medium confidence. Kalimati salgam quoted at NPR 50/kg and separately Rs 100/kg in different reports. Per this task's farm-gate-discount guidance, this entry uses NPR 1,800-2,500/quintal (~Rs 18-25/kg), discounted from the raw wholesale quotes and set somewhat below this file's radish entry (which is explicitly a red/white hybrid premium price).
Implied B:C ratio ~2.3 at these figures -- within this file's plausible range, and directionally consistent with (a bit lower than) radish's own ~1.7-2.2 ratio.

enterprises.name: Barley (Jau)
notes: Widest elevational range of any cereal in Nepal (Terai to ~4000m) but real cultivation concentrates in high-altitude districts like Jumla and Mustang -- unusually alkaline-tolerant (soil pH up to 8.5)

National yield is low (900 kg/ha) and no Nepal government MSP was found for barley (unlike wheat/paddy/millet) -- implied B:C is below 1, similar to this file's existing buckwheat (~0.67) and finger_millet (~0.77) hill-cereal entries, not a data error, reflecting a genuine low-cash, food-security/fodder-first hill staple
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plant id=71, source: 'Nepalese barley agro-morphology', ResearchGate) -- Mid-Hills: cultivated, high suitability, '5th most-cultivated Nepal cereal ... concentrated in high-altitude districts like Jumla'; High Hills: cultivated, high suitability, 'Jumla (2240-3000m), Mustang'; Mountain: marginal, low suitability, 'grown to ~4000m in places'. Env rows: soil_ph 6.0-8.5 (notes: 'unusually alkaline-tolerant'), optimal temp 15-20C, germinates from 4-5C soil temp

Season: Nepal-specific agronomy sources describe barley as a rabi crop sown mid-October to mid-November (late-sown varieties by December); a distinct high-altitude (~2300m) irrigated spring-sown variant exists (end-March to end-May) but the dominant Nepal pattern is winter/rabi (ResearchGate, 'Agro-morphological Variability of Barley under Normal and Late Sown Conditions in Chitwan, Nepal')

Yield: Nepal national average productivity 900 kg/ha (25,817 ha area, 23,224 MT production) -- Arthik Sandesh, 'Barley production in Nepal', citing government statistics; converts to ~3.6 quintal/acre. Used as-is (real, Nepal-specific, internally consistent figure)

Cost: NOT precisely researched -- no barley-specific Nepal cost-of-cultivation study was found despite several targeted searches (including a Dept. of Agriculture cereal cost/price-spread report that covers paddy/wheat but yielded no extractable barley figure). NPR 13,000/acre is this app's own estimate, set below the sourced millet figure (NPR 21,500/acre) to reflect barley's even lower Nepal yield and concentration on marginal, minimal-input high-altitude land -- low confidence

Price: no Nepal government MSP for barley was found (2026 MoALD MSP guidelines cover paddy/maize/wheat/millet but not barley), and retail Kathmandu/Pokhara prices (NPR 147-525/kg) look like a specialty-product markup, not farmgate. NPR 3,000-3,600/quintal is this app's own estimate, anchored at a discount to wheat's sourced NPR 3,945/quintal MSP -- low confidence

Cost: no Nepal source found. NPR 12,000/acre is this app's own estimate, below the sourced kodo/finger-millet figure (NPR 21,500/acre), reflecting a crop that per the DB is often not even deliberately cultivated -- low confidence

Yield: no Nepal-specific figure found. 3.0 quintal/acre (~0.75 t/ha) is estimated by analogy to this batch's other Nepal hill-millet yields (foxtail ~815 kg/ha, proso ~819-990 kg/ha), since barnyard millet is agronomically similar and general sources describe it as more a incidental/weedy presence than a managed crop in Nepal -- low confidence

enterprises.name: Foxtail Millet (Kaguno)
notes: Real, actively cultivated Karnali specialty grain, not just a subsistence filler: a trading company reportedly purchased 338 tons of kaguno in a recent year, and it is sold/exported under 'Karnali ko Kaguno' branding -- this supports a genuine price premium over generic millet (kodo), unlike most other crops in this batch
Nepal-specific productivity is nonetheless low (815 kg/ha) -- grown on marginal, non-irrigated mid/high-hill land (800-2800masl), often mixed-cropped with finger millet
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plant id=76, source: 'Karnali emerges as exporter of cereals', Kathmandu Post) -- Mid-Hills: cultivated, high suitability, '800-2500m, concentrated Karnali Province (Mugu, Kalikot, Humla, Jumla) plus Lamjung, Gorkha'; High Hills: cultivated, high suitability, 'Karnali districts extend into this belt'. No plant_environment_requirements rows exist for this species

Season/duration: Nepal-specific sources (krishisuchana.com) state kaguno is cultivated 800-2800masl and matures in 65-70 days; another Nepal-context source describes it as ready in 'three months' and 'harvested before the monsoon' -- used 80 days as a middle estimate; sown with the kharif millet group (Jun onset), consistent with this file's existing finger_millet/millet(kodo) entries

Yield: Nepal average productivity 815 kg/ha (krishisuchana.com), corroborated by a separate regional review giving foxtail millet ~0.99 t/ha -- used the more Nepal/Karnali-specific 815 kg/ha figure, converts to ~3.3 quintal/acre

Cost: no Nepal-specific figure found. NPR 15,500/acre is this app's own estimate, similar band to sourced kodo/millet cost (NPR 21,500/acre) but modestly lower given fully rainfed/non-irrigated cultivation -- low-medium confidence

Price: real Karnali local-market price found -- 'proso millet costs Rs160/kg, foxtail millet Rs150/kg' in Karnali local markets vs. up to Rs250/kg in Kathmandu (ekantipur.com, 'Karnali products from Japan to America'). NPR 12,000-15,000/quintal used, bracketing the Rs150/kg (=NPR 15,000/quintal) Karnali figure and allowing some farmgate discount below the local-market retail price -- medium confidence, real sourced anchor

sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plant id=79, source: 'Karnali emerges as exporter of cereals', Kathmandu Post) -- Mid-Hills only: cultivation_status MARGINAL, low agronomic suitability, evidence text verbatim: "Grouped generically under 'small millets' -- no distinct Nepal statistics found." Cost: no Nepal source found. NPR 13,000/acre is this app's own estimate, in line with this batch's other marginal small millets -- low confidence

enterprises.name: Oats (Jai)
notes: IMPORTANT: modeled as a FODDER crop, not a grain crop. Both the Nepal DB and multiple web sources agree oats in Nepal are grown 'almost exclusively as winter fodder' for livestock, with NARC having released ~6 fodder-specific oat varieties; packaged oat grain sold in Nepal shops (Kellogg's etc.) appears to be imported, not sourced from local grain markets

yieldPerUnit/priceMin/priceMax are therefore green-fodder tonnage and price (NPR per quintal fresh-cut, multi-cut winter season), NOT grain quintals -- not directly comparable to this file's other cereal entries on a per-quintal basis
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plant id=72, source: 'Nepalese barley agro-morphology', ResearchGate) -- Mid-Hills: cultivated, high suitability, evidence text verbatim: 'Grown almost exclusively as WINTER FODDER, not grain -- NARC released ~6 fodder oat varieties.' Env rows (general fallback, low confidence 0.3): temp -7 to 24C (optimal low 7C), rainfall 380-1140mm

Season: Nepal fodder-oat trials describe sowing in the third week of October through the first week of December (November being optimal) -- a winter (rabi) fodder crop; cold, dry climate considered ideal (Gandaki University fodder-oats trial; nepjol.info Journal of Agriculture and Natural Resources)

Yield: Nepal fodder trials report a first cut (~2 months after sowing) averaging 5-6 tons/ha green fodder, with a second cut by September reported at 8.11 tons/ha in one trial -- used ~10 t/ha (~100 quintal/ha, ~40 quintal/acre) as a rough total-season estimate across cuts -- low-medium confidence, real Nepal trial data but combined/extrapolated by this app

Cost: no Nepal cost figure found for fodder oats specifically. NPR 12,000/acre is this app's own low-input estimate (seed ~100kg/ha per NARC recommendation, minimal fertilizer, no threshing since cut green) -- low confidence

Price: no Nepal-specific green-fodder price found. NPR 500-700/quintal is this app's own estimate, anchored to an Indian green-fodder mandi rate of ~Rs280/quintal (=~NPR 450/quintal via the fixed 1 INR=1.6 NPR peg) with a modest premium for Nepal's cited winter fodder shortage -- low confidence, India-fallback-anchored

Cost/yield/price triangulated mostly from India dryland-farming studies (flagged fallback per task instructions) and scaled down substantially from India's more intensive/hybrid figures to reflect Nepal's much smaller and less-intensive cultivation -- treat as a rough directional estimate
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plant id=74, source: 'Nepalese barley agro-morphology', ResearchGate) -- Terai only: cultivation_status MARGINAL, low agronomic suitability, evidence text verbatim: "'Very limited' to small Terai/lower-hill areas; primarily an Indian dry-zone crop (Rajasthan/Gujarat/Haryana)." One web source's claimed '960-1000 day' maturity for chino was judged an almost-certain scraping/typo error and discarded -- proso millet is a fast-maturing cereal worldwide (60-100 days); duration set accordingly, well below this file's usual 90-150 day band

enterprises.name: Black Pepper (Marich)
notes: Real but genuinely niche Nepal cultivation -- the nepal_agri_ai DB rates it 'marginal' status / 'low' agronomic suitability ('virtually at nought'), but a 2025 Khabarhub feature on a real Gandaki-region grower, plus the DB's own cited district list (Morang, Sunsari, Jhapa in Terai; Ramechhap, Lamjung in the hills), shows real if scattered cultivation up to ~1,500m elevation -- wider than the DB's Terai-only framing.

NO Nepal per-acre cost/yield figure exists anywhere found. Economics below are built entirely from India/Kerala benchmarks (Kerala produces ~90% of India's pepper) as a stand-in, the same India-fallback approach this file already uses for litchi and coriander.
Slow-maturing perennial vine: ~5 years to first harvest, productive up to ~20 years -- like tea/litchi, this models an already-established, bearing planting, not a new one.
LOW-CONFIDENCE ENTRY. Include with caution; a real Nepal cost-of-cultivation study would meaningfully improve this estimate.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database, plant_region_suitability + regional_crops, Terai region, cultivation_status='marginal', agronomic_suitability='low': "'Virtually at nought' -- only sparse cultivation in Jhapa; bulk consumption imported from India." (source_id 200 -- note: that source_id's own stored title is 'Trend Analysis of Oilseed Crops Production in Nepal', a topic mismatch suggesting a mislabeled/reused citation in the underlying research; treated as lower-confidence for that reason). plant_environment_requirements had NO rows for this plant (no measured climate/soil bounds in the DB).

Cultivation extent (fresh web check, 2026): districts Morang, Sunsari, Jhapa, Ramechhap, Lamjung cited; real farmer case (Syangkhudi Tari, Pokhara Metropolitan City-28, Gandaki) growing pepper alongside 100+ support trees on a ~30-ropani mixed permaculture-style farm; 5 years to first harvest, productive up to 20 years; suitable up to 1,500m elevation, needs 2,000-3,000mm rainfall / 60-90% humidity. https://english.khabarhub.com/2025/03/473553/

Price: Nepal retail dried pepper Rs 2,000/kg cited in the same Khabarhub piece -- a retail, not farm-gate, figure. This entry's priceMin/Max (NPR 100,000-150,000/quintal = NPR 1,000-1,500/kg) sits below that retail figure and roughly brackets India domestic wholesale (₹400-1,200/kg per agrifarming.in and pepperhub.in, x~1.6 NPR:INR peg =~ NPR 640-1,920/kg) -- an estimate, not a direct Nepal citation.

Yield: India/Kerala benchmark -- 'an average well-managed acre produces 500-600 kg dried pepper' from 500-600 vines (agrifarming.in, pepperhub.in); this entry uses 6 quintal/acre (600kg), the upper end of that range, assuming a mature bearing planting. NOT a Nepal-specific figure.

Cost: NOT found for Nepal, nor as a clean India ANNUAL figure (only an India one-time establishment cost of ~₹1.5-2 lakh/acre was found). NPR 85,000/acre/year is this app's own estimate, by analogy to this file's other labor-intensive perennial entries (tea NPR 95,000; litchi NPR 136,000; large cardamom NPR 70,000/acre) -- unverified.

Sanity check: implied B:C = 6 x avg(100000,150000) / 85000 = 8.82. Higher than most of this file's field crops but the same order of magnitude as this file's own large_cardamom entry (B:C ~7.8, also a thin-supply high-value perennial spice) -- not treated as a unit-error flag, but the whole entry stays low-confidence given the total absence of direct Nepal cost/yield data.

enterprises.name: Cinnamon (Dalchini)
notes: The most marginal of this batch's INCLUDED entries -- the nepal_agri_ai DB and a fresh web check independently agree Nepal cinnamon is NOT an established plantation crop: it 'grows wild across hilly regions' with only 'recent, small-scale, still-nascent' organized cultivation by a handful of organic farms.

Every economics figure here is an estimate bridging Sri Lanka/India per-acre benchmarks (Nepal has none) -- treat this as the LOWEST-CONFIDENCE entry in this batch, more illustrative-of-potential than a verified current farm-gate picture.

Species is unspecified in the source data ('Cinnamomum spp.') -- may not be true Ceylon cinnamon (C. verum); could include cassia-type relatives, which typically trade at a lower price point than this entry assumes.
Perennial tree; bark harvest realistically starts around year 3+ per India data.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database, plant_region_suitability + regional_crops, Mid-Hills region, cultivation_status='marginal', agronomic_suitability='low': 'Grows wild across hilly regions; organized plantation cultivation is a recent, small-scale, still-nascent development.' (source_id 200 -- same mislabeled-source caveat as the black_pepper entry above). No plant_environment_requirements rows exist for this plant in the DB.

Cross-checked (fresh web check, 2026): confirms 'cinnamon wasn't commercially grown typically in Nepal though it could be seen growing wild in mid to high altitudes, recently few organic farms have started growing dalchini in small-scale' -- independent confirmation of nascent status. Also: Nepal exported ~1,978 tonnes / US$1.27M of cinnamon in 2022 (12th of 94 global exporters, 0.3% world share) -- note this export figure is plausibly re-exported/processed imported cinnamon rather than proof of domestic cultivation at that scale, given the same sources' cultivation description.

Yield: NOT found for Nepal. Sri Lanka/India benchmarks vary widely -- Sri Lanka ~300 kg/acre average (up to 600-700 kg/acre on a well-managed mature plantation); India figures ranging from ~22 kg/acre (very low, possibly poor-practice) up to ~150-225 kg/acre for 3-5 year-old trees. This entry uses 2.5 quintal/acre (250kg), toward the low end, reflecting Nepal's young/nascent plantings rather than a mature commercial estate -- this app's own estimate, not a direct citation.

Price: highly uncertain -- one source gives a bulk/wholesale price of ~US$0.64/kg (~NPR 85/kg), another gives Indian retail packaged spice at ~₹500/kg (~NPR 800/kg); these differ ~9x, plausibly wholesale-bulk vs. retail-packaged grades. This entry uses NPR 25,000-35,000/quintal (NPR 250-350/kg) as a rough farm-gate midpoint estimate between those two figures -- not a direct citation.

Cost: NOT found for Nepal. Sri Lanka cites only a 9-year total establishment project cost (~LKR 8.7M/ha, not a clean annual figure). NPR 40,000/acre/year is this app's own rough estimate for a low-input, small-scale/wild-adjacent planting, by analogy to large_cardamom's similarly low-input forest-understory NPR 70,000/acre entry -- unverified.

Sanity check: implied B:C = 2.5 x avg(25000,35000) / 40000 = 1.875. Deliberately modest/unexciting rather than inflated -- consistent with this crop's real documented 'marginal/nascent' status; the numbers are not dressed up to look more attractive than the underlying evidence supports.

enterprises.name: Fenugreek (Methi)
notes: The best-grounded AGRONOMIC entry in this batch -- the nepal_agri_ai DB has real, specific, multi-zone Nepal cultivation evidence: Kailali/Bardiya (Terai, Oct-Dec planting), Mid-Hills (Aug-Nov planting), and High-Hills (Mar-May planting), described in the source research as 'the most elevation-versatile spice researched.'

Modeled as SEED spice (methi seed), not leafy saag. The underlying source paper's own title calls fenugreek a 'climate risk resilient vegetable crop,' implying leaf/saag use is also significant in Nepal -- but this entry follows the task's 'spice crop' framing and uses seed yield/price economics. Gram's existing coriander entry already models the leafy-herb approach for a comparable crop, so this deliberately avoids duplicating that pattern; a future leaf-fenugreek entry could be added separately if needed.
Economics (cost/price) are India-fallback, NOT Nepal-specific -- no direct Nepal per-acre or per-quintal figure was found despite the real, confirmed Nepal cultivation.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database, plant_region_suitability + regional_crops, 3 real regional rows all cultivation_status='cultivated', agronomic_suitability='high': Terai 'Oct-Dec planting; Kailali, Bardiya districts'; Mid-Hills 'Aug-Nov planting'; High Hills 'Mar-May planting -- most elevation-versatile spice researched' (source_id 202, ResearchGate: 'Fenugreek: Review of Commercial Opportunities For A Climate Risk Resilient Vegetable Crop In Nepal'). plant_environment_requirements: temperature min 8C / optimal 16-22C / max 27C, frost-tolerant (confidence 0.5); soil_ph min 5.3 / optimal 6.0-7.0 / max 8.2 (confidence 0.4, itself flagged in the DB as a 'regional fallback' rather than a precise Nepal-measured value).

Seasons mapped as rabi (Terai Oct-Dec and Mid-Hills Aug-Nov -- both cool-season windows) plus zaid (High-Hills Mar-May -- a spring/early-summer window at altitude), spanning two of gram's three season buckets because real cultivation genuinely shifts window with elevation. This mirrors how this file already handles other crops with real multi-season evidence (e.g. litchi) honestly rather than forcing one bucket.

Yield: India benchmark -- seed yield 12-15 quintal/hectare (~4.9-6.1 quintal/acre after /2.471 conversion); this entry uses 5 quintal/acre, a rounded mid-estimate (general Indian agronomy sources, e.g. Package of Practice Fenugreek Cultivation). NOT Nepal-specific. Seeds mature 80-90 days after sowing -- durationDays set to 90.

Cost: India benchmark -- a Bikaner (Rajasthan) district economic study gives cost ₹37,380/ha (cash-basis; B:C ratio 1.70 in that study); another India source gives a more comprehensive ₹95,434/ha (fuller-cost basis). This entry uses NPR 32,000/acre, close to the lower cash-cost end (₹37,380/ha x1.6 NPR:INR /2.471 acre/ha =~ NPR 24,200/acre) with some margin added -- consistent with this file's stated preference for cash-basis over full-economic-cost figures (see rice's own sourcing note on this exact point). NOT a Nepal citation.

Price: India benchmark -- mandi (wholesale) methi seed price ~₹5,880.86/quintal (commodityonline.com, 2026 data), x~1.6 NPR:INR peg =~ NPR 9,410/quintal. This entry uses NPR 8,500-10,500/quintal. NOT a Nepal citation -- no Nepal-specific quintal price was found despite the real, confirmed Nepal cultivation.

Sanity check: implied B:C = 5 x avg(8500,10500) / 32000 = 1.48. Modest and realistic for a cheap seed-commodity spice, in the same family as this file's well-grounded cereal crops rather than an inflated spice-premium number -- appropriate given fenugreek seed is a bulk commodity, not a rare high-value spice.

enterprises.name: Chrysanthemum (Godawari)
notes: Real, well-established Nepal cultivation -- Godawari (in Lalitpur) is literally the Nepali name for this flower and home to the Floriculture Association Nepal; a secondary presence exists around Kaski/Pokhara. A 2024 Kathmandu Post piece notes Nepal has reached self-sufficiency in chrysanthemum production for Tihar.

ECONOMICS ARE NOT DIRECTLY SOURCED. Despite several searches, no chrysanthemum-specific Nepal (or India) per-acre cost/yield/price figure was found -- only garland-level anecdotes (Rs 3,000/garland at Tihar peak; one grower's real account of expecting Rs 200,000 but earning only Rs 30,000 due to an unsold-flower glut). This entry's cost/yield/price fields are built ENTIRELY by structural analogy to gram's own marigold entry (same open-field smallholder cut/loose-flower system, same Tihar-driven demand cycle), with price nudged upward to reflect chrysanthemum's generally higher per-unit market value. Flag this as unverified, on par with how this file's tea/large_cardamom entries already flag their own un-researched cost fields -- not a directly cited figure.
Modeled on the same kharif (Jun-sow, Nov-harvest, Tihar-timed) cycle as marigold given the shared festival-driven demand window.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database, plant_region_suitability + regional_crops: Mid-Hills, cultivation_status='cultivated', agronomic_suitability='high': 'Godawari, Lalitpur (namesake of the Nepali name); Floriculture Association Nepal founded there'; Inner Terai, cultivation_status='marginal', agronomic_suitability='low': 'Kaski/Pokhara secondary presence' (source_id 211, stored as RJOAS 'Production, Marketing and Economic Analysis of Marigold Production in Nepal' -- note this source is titled as a marigold-specific paper being cited for chrysanthemum data, likely a floriculture-sector paper with comparative flower-crop discussion; treated as reasonably credible given the specific, checkable place/institution names, but flagged for the title mismatch). plant_environment_requirements: temperature optimal_low 15C, max 28C (night 15-20C during bud formation), confidence 0.4.

Cross-checked (fresh web check, 2026): Kathmandu Post, 'Nepali flower farmers thrive as Indian imports restricted during Tihar' (Nov 2024) -- confirms real commercial chrysanthemum/Godawari cultivation, ~100,000 garlands expected at one recent Tihar, garlands up to Rs 3,000 each at peak; also reports a real grower earning only Rs 30,000 against an expected Rs 200,000 due to an unsold-flower glut -- cited here as qualitative evidence for this entry's priceVolatility rating, not as a per-acre figure. https://kathmandupost.com/national/2024/11/02/nepali-flower-farmers-thrive-as-indian-imports-restricted-during-tihar

Cost/Yield/Price: NOT found for chrysanthemum specifically, Nepal or India. This entry estimates costPerUnit NPR 35,000/acre (marigold's real NPR 22,520/acre plus a margin for chrysanthemum's typically more labor-intensive disbudding/staking), yieldPerUnit 65 quintal/acre (below marigold's real 121.4 quintal/acre, reflecting chrysanthemum's smaller flower head), and priceMin/Max NPR 1,200-1,800/quintal (above marigold's real NPR 600-800/quintal, reflecting chrysanthemum's higher per-unit value implied by the Rs 3,000/garland figure) -- ALL THREE fields are this app's own unverified estimate, not cited figures.

Sanity check: implied B:C = 65 x avg(1200,1800) / 35000 = 2.79. Deliberately kept BELOW marigold's own well-grounded B:C of 3.786 (this file's best-documented flower study) given this entry's much weaker sourcing -- avoids overstating confidence via an inflated ratio.

enterprises.name: Gladiolus
notes: Real, well-documented Nepal cultivation -- the nepal_agri_ai DB has specific dual-zone evidence with genuinely counter-cyclical planting windows: Terai (Jhapa, Chitwan, Morang; Dec-Jan planting) and Mid-Hills (Kathmandu Valley, Bhaktapur, Lalitpur; May-Jul planting). Nepal's 2nd most important cut flower per multiple sources, with a stated comparative cost/quality advantage over Indian imports.

Yield figure is back-calculated from a real national aggregate (800,000 sticks/year from 340 ropani, a Nepal floriculture blog figure) rather than a direct per-acre citation -- the arithmetic is shown transparently in sources below so it can be checked.

Price is NOT Nepal-sourced -- no reliable NPR per-stem figure was found. Indian mandi 'per quintal' cut-flower listings found (₹50-70/quintal) were implausibly low and clearly unusable for a stem-counted crop -- disregarded as bad/junk data, consistent with this project's history of catching exactly this kind of unit-mismatch error. This entry's price is instead estimated by comparison to gram's own rose entry (NPR 8-20/stem), set somewhat lower to reflect gladiolus's typically lower per-stem value than rose.

Modeled as a single ~90-100 day planting-to-harvest cycle (bulb/corm crop), NOT a year-round perennial like gram's rose entry -- durationDays and cost reflect ONE cycle, not an established-planting annual figure. A grower could potentially run more than one cycle per year using the Terai/hills counter-cyclical windows noted above, which this single-cycle economics figure does not capture.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database, plant_region_suitability + regional_crops: Terai, cultivation_status='cultivated', agronomic_suitability='high': 'Jhapa, Chitwan, Morang -- Dec-Jan planting window (counter-cyclical to hills)'; Mid-Hills, cultivation_status='cultivated', agronomic_suitability='high': 'Kathmandu Valley, Bhaktapur, Lalitpur -- May-Jul planting window' (source_id 211, see chrysanthemum entry above for this source's title-mismatch caveat). plant_environment_requirements: temperature min 6C / optimal max 20C / max 26C, night should not exceed 16C (confidence 0.7, 'Nepal-specific source'); soil_ph optimal 5.5-6.5 (confidence 0.6, 'Nepal-specific source') -- among the HIGHER-confidence environmental data in this whole batch.

Cross-checked (fresh web check, 2026): confirms cultivation concentrated in 'Kathmandu, Bhaktapur, Lalitpur, Jhapa and Chitwan'; national demand '6,000-8,000 sticks per day'; 'second most important cut flower in Nepal with comparative advantage for cost and quality production over India'; 70-90 days from planting to flowering. https://ecominions2014.wordpress.com/gladiolus-cultivation-challenges-and-demand-in-nepal/

Yield: back-calculated from the same source's national figures -- '800,000 sticks per annum' from '340 ropani' nationally. Ropani-to-acre conversion: 1 ropani = 5,476 sq ft = 0.1257 acre, so 340 ropani = 42.7 acres. 800,000 sticks / 42.7 acres =~ 18,720 sticks/acre, rounded to 18,700. (NOTE: an earlier draft of this same calculation mistakenly used 1 ropani = 0.0508 acre, which understates the true value by ~2.5x and would have overstated yield to ~46,300 sticks/acre -- corrected before finalizing; flagged here explicitly since this project has repeatedly found and fixed exactly this class of unit-conversion bug.) A different, seemingly-inconsistent figure in the same source ('10,000-120,000 plants... per ropani') looks internally garbled (its upper end implies an implausible planting density) and was NOT used.

Price: NOT found as a usable Nepal or India figure (the only India mandi listings found, ₹50-70/quintal for cut gladiolus, are almost certainly a data error for a crop that is sold by the stem, not by weight -- not used). This entry estimates NPR 7-13/stem by comparison to gram's own rose entry (NPR 8-20/stem, itself flagged in that entry as this file's least-resolved cost/price correction) -- an unverified estimate.

Cost: NOT found for Nepal or India on a clean per-acre basis. NPR 70,000/acre/cycle is this app's own estimate reflecting a moderate-input bulb crop (corm cost + land prep + staking + irrigation) over a single ~90-100 day cycle -- well below rose's year-round NPR 350,000/acre given gladiolus's much shorter cycle and lack of greenhouse infrastructure -- unverified.

Sanity check: implied B:C = 18700 x avg(7,13) / 70000 = 2.67. Comparable to marigold's real 3.79 and below rose's own (still shaky) ~3.6 -- reasonable given gladiolus's real 'second most important cut flower' status, without leaning on the unreliable India per-quintal price data.

enterprises.name: Aloe Vera (Ghiukumari)
notes: Real, named-district Nepal cultivation (Banke, Bardiya, Kailali, Rupandehi, Kapilvastu, Nawalparasi, Chitwan per nepal_agri_ai's source) sold into an export-oriented herbal-oil/gel supply chain, but no Nepal-specific cost/yield/price study was found -- economics below are an India-analogy estimate (flagged field-by-field), not Nepal-verified like the zones/regional-cultivation claim is.
Drought-tolerant (only ~350-400mm rainfall needed per the DB's environment-requirement row) -- modeled as rainfed only.

Perennial succulent, harvestable for several years once established -- durationDays set to 365 (occupies land year-round) following this file's existing convention for banana/cardamom/tea rather than a literal single-cycle length.
sources: Agronomic data (zones/regional cultivation/temperature/rainfall): nepal_agri_ai database, plant_environment_requirements + plant_region_suitability for plant_id=136, citing Nepali Times 'Now, Nepal's herbal oil in Europe' -- Terai (Banke/Bardiya/Kailali/Rupandehi/Kapilvastu/Nawalparasi/Chitwan) and Inner Terai (Dhading) both rated 'high' agronomic suitability and 'cultivated'.

Cost: NOT Nepal-sourced. India analogy: ~INR 75,000/acre/year established-planting maintenance cost (agrifarming.in / krishijagran.com-class sources), converted to NPR at the ~1.6x peg -> ~NPR 120,000/acre. Low-medium confidence.
Yield: India analogy, 15-24 tonnes fresh leaf/acre/year cited across multiple India farming guides; this entry uses a conservative 15 tonnes (150 quintal)/acre. Not Nepal-verified.

Price: India analogy, contract-farming buyback quotes of INR 15-30/kg fresh leaf (mittigoldorganic.com, agriworldview.com), converted to NPR at 1.6x -> NPR 2,400-4,800/quintal. A Kathmandu-valley RETAIL price of NPR 999/kg (onlinetarkaripasal.com) was found but explicitly excluded as a consumer, not farm-gate, price.
Implied B:C ratio ~4.5 (revenue ~NPR 540,000 vs cost NPR 120,000) -- plausible for a contract-farmed export-oriented crop, not flagged as suspicious.

enterprises.name: Ashwagandha (Winter Cherry)
notes: IMPORTANT: this entry overrides the DB's own low-confidence read. The nepal_agri_ai plant_region_suitability row for Ashwagandha says cultivation was 'not_found_after_search' (citing a peer-reviewed Chitwan study claiming Nepal depends on India for raw material) -- but that row was sourced from a generic Nepali Times herbal-oil article not really about Ashwagandha. A targeted search for this batch found a much more specific, on-topic Kathmandu Post story (2017) confirming real commercial cultivation in Rupandehi district (Mayadevi Rural Municipality) via a farmer cooperative -- used as the zones basis instead.

That same Kathmandu Post article contains a dramatic anecdote (one farmer earning NPR 2.1 million on 1 bigha vs NPR 150,000/year from wheat/paddy, cooperative paying NPR 3,000/kg) that reads as a best-case promotional testimonial, not a typical-farmer average -- back-calculating yield/cost from it alone produced an implausible >25x B:C ratio. This entry instead uses conservative India-analogy root-yield/cost figures and treats the Nepal article's price/income claims as corroborating upside, noted but not directly used.

80 Ayurvedic drug companies in Nepal reportedly buy ~NPR 1 billion/year of ashwagandha combined, per the same article, suggesting real domestic demand even though supply is still partly import-dependent from India.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database, plant_region_suitability for plant_id=137 (Terai row, low confidence, 'not_found_after_search') -- superseded for zones purposes by a fresh, more specific web source (see notes).

Zones/cultivation evidence: Kathmandu Post, 'High returns lure farmers to growing ashwagandha' (2017) -- confirms real commercial cultivation, Rupandehi district, cooperative offtake at NPR 3,000/kg, ~6 months to first harvest.

Cost: NOT Nepal-verified. India-analogy rainfed cultivation cost ~INR 28,000-31,000/acre (standard Indian ag-extension package-of-practice figures for this low-input dryland crop), converted at 1.6x -> ~NPR 45,000-50,000/acre. Medium-low confidence.
Yield: India-analogy, ~300-400 kg dry root/acre under rainfed conditions per Indian agronomic literature; this entry uses 350 kg (3.5 quintal)/acre. Medium confidence.

Price: NPR 30,000-55,000/quintal (NPR 300-550/kg) is a compromise between conservative India farm-gate dry-root price analogies (~NPR 240-400/kg after conversion) and the higher Nepal-specific NPR 3,000-4,000/kg figures found (which likely reflect seed or premium/export grade rather than bulk dry root, and were not used directly to avoid the inflated B:C ratio described in notes).
Duration: 180 days (~6 months to first harvest) directly from the Kathmandu Post article, cross-consistent with standard Indian Ashwagandha root-harvest timelines (150-180 days).
Implied B:C ratio ~2.98 (revenue ~NPR 148,750 vs cost NPR 50,000) -- deliberately kept conservative; treat as a floor rather than a ceiling given the real Nepal price signals ran higher.

enterprises.name: Chiraito (Swertia chirayita)

Kept as-is (900 days, the midpoint) rather than 'corrected' down.

High-hills only (1700-3000m core commercial belt: Ilam, Panchthar, Taplejung, Sankhuwasabha, Bhojpur, per the DB's regional_crops evidence, 25-year cultivation history) -- a separate Mountain-zone row exists but is wild-collection only ('low' agronomic suitability, elevation 3000-5500m), not cultivation, so not used to justify a broader zone.

enterprises.name: Lemongrass (Kaghati Jhar)

Flagged as medium confidence.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database, plant_environment_requirements + plant_region_suitability for plant_id=134, citing Nepali Times 'Now, Nepal's herbal oil in Europe' -- Terai and Inner Terai rated 'high' suitability/cultivated, Mid-Hills rated 'low'/marginal but real (named districts).

enterprises.name: Mint (Pudina)
notes: Modeled as an essential-oil crop like lemongrass, following the same real Nepal source (Nawalparasi West cooperative sells mint oil at NPR 4,000/liter, which anchors this entry's price) rather than fresh-leaf, since Nepal's documented commercial mint economy in this data is oil-based, not a large-scale industrial mentha-oil operation like India's Uttar Pradesh belt.

Water-loving relative to this batch's other herbs -- the DB's soil_ph row and 'damp fertile soils of mid-hill regions' note both point to consistent moisture needs, reflected in a higher waterDependency score than lemongrass/aloe.
Real cultivation confirmed in Terai (Nawalparasi West community forest) and Mid-Hills (damp fertile soils, 'high' suitability in both) -- no Inner Terai or High-Hills evidence found either way.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database, plant_environment_requirements + plant_region_suitability for plant_id=135, citing Nepali Times 'Now, Nepal's herbal oil in Europe' -- Terai and Mid-Hills both rated 'high' suitability/cultivated.

Price: NPR 4,000/liter is a real, Nepal-specific cooperative-level oil price from the same source article (100 liters/year group production, Nawalparasi West). priceMin/Max (NPR 3,500-4,500) brackets this single data point since no second Nepal source was found to corroborate a range. Medium confidence.

Yield: 30 L oil/acre/year is this batch's own conservative estimate by analogy with the lemongrass entry's small-scale community-cooperative production model (rather than India's industrial mentha-oil yields of 80-120 L/acre, judged not representative of Nepal's current small-holder scale). Low-medium confidence, flagged as an estimate.
Cost: NOT Nepal-verified. Estimated by analogy with lemongrass (a comparable-scale perennial oil herb), scaled down slightly for mint's lower biomass -- NPR 45,000/acre/year. Low confidence.
