enterprises.name: Stevia (Stevia rebaudiana)
notes: LOWEST-CONFIDENCE entry in this batch. The DB itself describes Nepal cultivation as pilot/trial status only ('Bhaktapur/Madhyapur Thimi commercial trial. Dolakha district cited as suitable (500-2500m) but not confirmed planted'), with 'low' agronomic suitability and no confirmed scaled production anywhere in Nepal. This entry should be read as 'agronomically possible, commercially unproven in Nepal' rather than an established cash crop like the other five herbs in this batch.

All economics figures are India-analogy (no Nepal cost/yield/price data exists to research, pilot-stage only) and additionally discounted below the India literature's figures to avoid overstating a market with no demonstrated Nepal buyer network -- yield in particular uses ~12 quintal/acre/year vs. India sources' cited 15-27 quintal/acre/year range.

priceVolatility and waterDependency both set high (4) reflecting genuine uncertainty (no established offtake market in Nepal) and the crop's real intolerance of moisture stress, respectively; capitalLockIn set to 3 (moderate) rather than higher, since agronomically first harvest comes relatively quickly (~90-120 days) even though the broader commercial viability is unproven.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database, plant_region_suitability for plant_id=139 (Mid-Hills only, 'low' agronomic suitability, cultivation_status='marginal'/pilot), citing Nepali Times 'Now, Nepal's herbal oil in Europe'. No plant_environment_requirements rows exist for this crop in the DB (0 rows).

Cost: NOT Nepal-verified. India analogy, year-2-onward established maintenance cost ~INR 15,000-20,000/acre plus a margin for Nepal's less mature input-supply chain -> NPR 45,000/acre/year used here (toward the higher end of the converted India range). Low confidence.

Yield: India analogy, 1,500-2,700 kg dried leaf/acre/year cited across Indian stevia-farming sources (400-600 kg per cut, 3-4 cuts/year); this entry uses a discounted 1,200 kg (12 quintal)/acre/year given Nepal's unproven, non-scaled cultivation status. Low confidence, deliberately conservative.

Price: India analogy, documented dried-leaf contract buyback prices of INR 55-100/kg, converted at 1.6x -> NPR 8,800-16,000/quintal (NPR 88-160/kg); used directly as NPR 9,000-16,000/quintal. Low-medium confidence.

Implied B:C ratio ~3.33 (revenue ~NPR 150,000 vs cost NPR 45,000) -- reasonable on paper, but given the pilot-only cultivation status, treat this whole entry as more speculative than its B:C ratio alone suggests.

enterprises.name: Cotton (Kapas)
notes: A real but genuinely marginal and declining Terai crop, not a data error -- the DB's own regional_crops evidence (already researched, ResearchGate 'Research Advancement of Cotton in Nepal') states cultivation is now confined to ~122.5 ha nationally (Banke/Bardiya/Dang), down from ~3,600 ha in 1995/96, with 'poor profitability -- mills prefer cheaper imported cotton/yarn, no support price', and the Cotton Development Board was dissolved in FY 2080/81.

The resulting B:C ratio here (~1.05, barely above breakeven) is a DELIBERATE reflection of that documented poor-profitability narrative, not a sign of a unit-mismatch bug -- it was cross-checked specifically because a ratio this thin looks suspicious, but it lines up with the sourced real-world decline story.

No Nepal-specific farm-gate price for raw seed cotton (kapas) was found; a Nepal 'export unit value' of USD 4.08/kg (NPR ~541/kg) exists but was explicitly rejected as a price basis here since it prices a processed/export lint product, not raw farm-gate kapas, and using it would have produced an absurd B:C ratio -- exactly the per-kg-vs-per-quintal / processed-vs-raw trap this batch was warned about.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database, plant_environment_requirements + plant_region_suitability for plant_id=43, citing ResearchGate 'Research Advancement of Cotton in Nepal' -- Terai only, 'low' agronomic suitability, cultivation_status='marginal', yield 1,118 kg seed cotton/ha.
Yield: 4.5 quintal/acre directly converted from the DB's cited 1,118 kg/ha (seed cotton/kapas) figure -- this is the best-grounded figure in this entry (Nepal-specific, already-researched).

Cost: NOT Nepal-verified. India analogy for rainfed/semi-irrigated cotton, ~INR 25,000-30,000/acre cultivation cost from general Indian cost-of-cultivation literature, converted at 1.6x -> ~NPR 45,000/acre. Low confidence.

Price: NOT a direct Nepal farm-gate figure. Uses India's Cotton Corporation of India-adjacent MSP-era kapas price (~INR 7,000-7,500/quintal for medium staple in recent seasons) converted at 1.6x (-> ~NPR 11,000-12,000/quintal), then set slightly below that (NPR 9,000-12,000/quintal) to reflect Nepal's explicitly-documented lack of any support price and weaker mill demand. Low confidence, directionally reasoned rather than directly sourced.
Implied B:C ratio ~1.05 (revenue ~NPR 47,250 vs cost NPR 45,000) -- thin on purpose; see notes.

enterprises.name: Black Gram (Kalo Dal/Mas)
notes: Real, DB-confirmed Nepal pulse grown across a wide elevation band (Terai up to Jumla) -- known locally as 'maas', a staple kharif/monsoon pulse distinct from this file's rabi pulses (lentil, chickpea)
Short-duration nitrogen-fixing rotation crop, similar rotation role to mungbean but sown at monsoon onset (kharif) rather than the pre-monsoon zaid window mungbean fills
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database. plant_region_suitability rows (plant_id=82): Terai (elevation 60-300m) and Mid-Hills (elevation 1000-2000m), both cultivation_status='cultivated', agronomic_suitability='high', regional_cultivation=1. Evidence text: '150-2850m range (Terai up to Jumla)' (Terai row) and 'Also grown here' (Mid-Hills row). Source: PMC black gram genetics/genomics paper (source_id 192, pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10822891). plant_environment_requirements (same source, knowledge_confidence 0.3, labeled 'Regional fallback' i.e. generic-crop values not Nepal-specific): temperature min 8C / optimal 25-35C / max 40C; soil_ph min 4.5 / optimal 6-7 / max 7.5 -- used to justify tolerance of a range of soils (loamy/sandy-loam/alluvial) rather than a narrow alluvial-only pick.

Season: Nepal is stated directly in a general black-gram cultivation guide as growing 'maas' in the kharif/rainy and summer season (krishijagran.com Black Gram Cultivation calendar; agrifarming.in). Best kharif sowing window given as 2nd fortnight of July (15-30 Jul), full window mid-June to mid-August. Duration 90 days used as a representative short-to-medium black gram maturity figure (India sources give ~70-100 days depending on variety); no Nepal-specific variety-duration study was found, so this is a South-Asia-typical figure, not a Nepal citation.

Cost: NPR 12,500/acre -- ESTIMATE, medium confidence. No direct Nepal cost-of-cultivation figure was found. Anchored between this file's real Nepal lentil figure (NPR 12,000/acre, Terai farmer-practice survey) and an India black-gram cost study (~INR 18,702/ha total cultivation expense = ~INR 7,568/acre -> NPR 12,110/acre at the 1.6 peg) -- the two anchors land within ~5% of each other, which is reassuring even though neither is a direct Nepal black-gram citation.

Yield: 2.8 quintal/acre -- ESTIMATE, medium confidence. India's own national average yield is low (681 kg/ha per agrifarming.in, i.e. ~276 kg/acre = 2.76 quintal/acre); 'well-managed'/irrigated figures of 12-15 quintal/ha (~4.9-6.1 quintal/acre) were judged too optimistic for a rainfed Nepal smallholder crop and NOT used, consistent with this project's practice of preferring realistic-farmer-field over best-case trial figures. 2.8 quintal/acre rounds the India national-average conversion.

Price: NPR 12,000-14,000/quintal -- ESTIMATE, medium confidence, India MSP/market-anchored. India's 2025-26 kharif MSP for urad (black gram) is INR 7,800/quintal (up INR 400 from the prior year, PIB press release); a separate current mandi price check found India black-gram-dal averaging INR 7,700-8,006/quintal. Converting the MSP at the fixed 1.6 peg gives ~NPR 12,480/quintal, which this range brackets. Treated as a calibration anchor, not a direct Nepal price -- no Nepal-specific mas/black-gram farmgate price survey was found.
Sanity check: implied B:C = 2.8 x avg(12000,14000) / 12500 = 2.91 -- in the same band as this file's real lentil (~3.7) and chickpea (~4.0) pulses, not an outlier.

enterprises.name: Field Pea (Matar)
notes: This is the DRY GRAIN/pulse form of pea, agronomically and economically distinct from gram's existing 'garden_pea' entry (fresh green-pod vegetable crop, hills-only, priced ~NPR 3,200-8,500/quintal by weight including pod) -- do not confuse the two when integrating

Grown in the Terai mainly as post-rice 'utera'/relay cropping: seed broadcast into standing rice shortly before rice harvest, then matures on residual soil moisture with no separate irrigation or land preparation -- the same low-input pattern as this file's existing lentil entry
Mid-Hills presence is real but explicitly marginal ('limited to warmer pockets' per the DB) -- Terai is the primary zone
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database. plant_region_suitability rows (plant_id=84): Terai (elevation 60-300m), cultivation_status='cultivated', agronomic_suitability='high', regional_cultivation=1, evidence: "Post-rice utera/relay cropping on residual moisture -- the dry/grain-market form of the same species as this file's 'Garden pea' (fresh-vegetable form)"; Mid-Hills (elevation 1000-2000m), agronomic_suitability='low', regional_cultivation=1, evidence: 'Limited to warmer pockets.' Source: Vikaspedia pigeon pea package of practices (source_id 191, agriculture.vikaspedia.in -- labeled in the DB itself as 'India, regional fallback', i.e. lower confidence / cross-referenced rather than a dedicated field-pea study).

Season: rabi, consistent with the DB's own utera/relay-cropping description and with this file's precedent for other Terai utera/residual-moisture rabi pulses (lentil: Oct sow / Feb harvest / 105 days). No dedicated Nepal field-pea sowing-date study was found, so the Oct-Feb / 105-day window is taken directly by analogy to lentil's real, grounded Nepal calendar rather than independently sourced -- flag as medium confidence. A general South Asian rabi-pulse guide (eagri.org lecture notes) separately confirms Oct-end-to-mid-Nov sowing for field pea, consistent with this window.

Cost: NPR 11,000/acre -- ESTIMATE, medium-low confidence, set slightly below this file's real lentil figure (NPR 12,000/acre) to reflect utera's typically near-zero separate land-preparation cost (broadcast into an already-prepared rice field) -- no direct Nepal field-pea cost-of-cultivation study was found.

Yield: 4.0 quintal/acre -- ESTIMATE, medium confidence. An India source states field pea 'average productivity ... 1.4 t/ha' for dry grain (i.e. ~0.567 t/acre = 5.67 quintal/acre once converted at 1 ha = 2.4711 acre) as a national-average figure (the same source's much higher '10-11 tonnes/hectare' figure is clearly for fresh green pods, a different product, and was excluded). 4.0 quintal/acre is set somewhat below that India national-average conversion, reasoning that Nepal's utera/relay method is lower-input than a dedicated sole-cropped field pea and should undershoot India's own average, similar to how this file's lentil (4.2 quintal/acre) and chickpea (4.5 quintal/acre) sit for the same cropping system.

Price: NPR 7,500-9,000/quintal -- ESTIMATE, medium-low confidence, ratio-derived rather than directly sourced. India dry-pea/matar mandi prices found were widely scattered (INR 2,582-5,678/quintal 'Field Pea', INR 4,935-5,222/quintal 'Peas (Dry)', with an INR 10,200/quintal outlier) -- taking a representative India dry-pea price of roughly INR 4,500-5,500/quintal against a representative India masur/lentil-equivalent price of roughly INR 6,500-7,500/quintal gives a ratio of ~0.70-0.75x; applying that ratio to this file's real, grounded Nepal lentil price (NPR 10,000-11,000/quintal) yields ~NPR 7,000-8,250/quintal, which this range brackets (shifted slightly upward for a small margin of safety). As a loose secondary sanity check only (different product, NOT used as the basis): fresh green Kalimati kerau retails NPR 70-85/kg (NPR 7,000-8,500/quintal by coincidence similar order of magnitude, per Kalimati wholesale listings), though fresh pod and dry grain are not directly comparable products.

Sanity check: implied B:C = 4.0 x avg(7500,9000) / 11000 = 3.00 -- comfortably inside this file's real lentil (~3.7) / chickpea (~4.0) band, and appropriately below both given field pea's lower per-quintal price.

enterprises.name: Faba Bean (Bakullo)
notes: LOWEST-CONFIDENCE entry in this batch. The DB itself flags this as a minor home-garden hill legume with 'no MoALD statistics found' -- real cultivation exists (regional_cultivation=1) but Nepal does not track it as an organized commercial crop, so all three economics figures below are analogy-based estimates rather than citations
Large-seeded, cool-season winter legume grown up to ~1800m in hill farming systems -- agronomically closer to this file's chickpea (long-duration rabi pulse) than to the shorter-cycle lentil
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database. plant_region_suitability row (plant_id=87): Mid-Hills (elevation 1000-2000m), cultivation_status='marginal', agronomic_suitability='low', regional_cultivation=1, evidence: 'Grown up to 1800m in hill farming systems, essentially a minor/home-garden legume -- no MoALD statistics found.' Season: no Nepal-specific faba bean planting calendar was found. Rabi/winter placement follows directly from the crop's known cool-season biology (optimal 15-18C per harvesttotable.com growing guide) and from the DB's own Mid-Hills 'winter hill legume' framing; the Oct-Mar / 150-day window is set by analogy to this file's chickpea (a similarly large-seeded, longer-duration rabi hill/Terai pulse at 148 days) rather than independently sourced. (Nepal's aggregate 'beans' FAOSTAT category, 0.085 t/ha nationally per one search result, mixes many bean species and was judged too broad/contaminated to use directly.)

India 'Broad Beans' mandi listings found (~INR 5,980/quintal national average, INR 2,750-4,500/quintal in Gujarat) are very likely FRESH green broad bean (vegetable) prices given typical mandi-tracker categorization, not dry faba/bakullo grain -- flagged explicitly and NOT used as the basis, to avoid the same fresh-vs-dry mismatch this batch deliberately avoided for field pea.

Sanity check: implied B:C = 4.0 x avg(10500,12500) / 12000 = 3.83 -- close to this file's real chickpea (~4.0), which is the intended read given how directly this estimate leans on the chickpea/lentil analogy; treat the whole economics block as a directional placeholder pending real Nepal data, not a verified figure.

enterprises.name: Linseed (Alas)
notes: Real, DB-confirmed Mid-Hills winter oilseed, best-documented in Lamjung District, typically grown alongside/grouped with mustard as a rabi oilseed rotation option

Yield is the best-grounded figure in this entry -- a real Nepal (FAOSTAT-sourced) national figure, not an estimate -- but it is a genuinely low per-acre yield; this is a marginal, low-input hill oilseed, not a high-output crop
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database. plant_region_suitability row (plant_id=91): Mid-Hills (elevation 1000-2000m), cultivation_status='cultivated', agronomic_suitability='high', regional_cultivation=1, evidence: 'Best-documented example Lamjung District; grouped with mustard as a winter oilseed crop.' plant_environment_requirements row: growing_duration_days optimal_low=90 / optimal_high=125 days, knowledge_confidence 0.6, notes 'Cool, short growing season.' Source for both: 'Flax production in Nepal' (source_id 199, Wikipedia, citing FAOSTAT) -- a genuinely Nepal-specific, if secondary-aggregator, source.

Season: rabi, following the DB's own 'grouped with mustard' framing -- this file's real mustard entry sows Ashoj-Mangsir (~Oct) and harvests Magh-Falgun (~Feb), a ~100-110 day window matching linseed's own DB-sourced 90-125 day duration closely. Duration set to 110 days, within the DB's real 90-125 day range.

Two India studies: cost of cultivation ~INR 19,129/ha across 5 varieties, and ~INR 17,598/ha at 50% recommended fertilizer dose (a plausible proxy for Nepal's likely lower-input hill practice) -- converting the lower figure (INR 17,598/ha = INR 7,122/acre) at the 1.6 peg gives ~NPR 11,395/acre, which this figure rounds up from slightly.

Yield: 2.1 quintal/acre -- a real Nepal figure (medium-high confidence), not estimated. Nepal reported flax yields of 5000 Hg/ha (2012) and 5358 Hg/ha (2013) per Wikipedia/FAOSTAT (1 hectogram = 100g, so 500-536 kg/ha) -- converting at 1 ha = 2.4711 acre gives ~202-217 kg/acre = ~2.0-2.2 quintal/acre. This is notably lower than mustard's real Nepal yield (4.5 quintal/acre), consistent with linseed being the more marginal, less-optimized of the two 'grouped' winter oilseeds.

Price: NPR 9,500-12,500/quintal -- ESTIMATE, medium-low confidence. Nepal flaxseed IMPORT prices (Tridge) ranged USD 0.61-0.74/kg (2023) and USD 0.61-0.87/kg (2024); converting at an approximate USD/NPR rate of ~135 gives roughly NPR 82-118/kg = NPR 8,200-11,800/quintal. This is an import/landed price, not a farmgate price, so it likely somewhat overstates what a Nepal grower actually receives -- used as a rough ceiling-anchor rather than a direct farmgate citation; no direct Nepal linseed farmgate price study was found.

Sanity check: implied B:C = 2.1 x avg(9500,12500) / 12000 = 1.93 -- below this file's lentil/chickpea band but similar in shape to this file's real sesame entry (B:C ~2.4, also a marginal/secondary oilseed on poorer land) and still comfortably inside the 1.5-4 target band, not an outlier.

enterprises.name: Castor (Andi)
notes: SECOND-LOWEST-CONFIDENCE entry in this batch (after faba bean). The DB explicitly describes Nepal castor as 'Subsistence/incidental only -- fallow land, field margins; household oil/folk medicine use, not organized commercial farming' -- this is real cultivation, but not commercial-scale, so all economics figures are India-analog estimates scaled down, not Nepal citations

Longest-duration crop in this batch (~165 days) -- a long-season crop grown on marginal/fallow land rather than dedicated prime cropland in its actual current Nepal use pattern; treat the per-acre economics as illustrative of what a dedicated planting could look like, not as a description of how it is typically grown today
Drought-tolerant and genuinely low-water, consistent with its field-margin/fallow-land niche
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database. plant_region_suitability row (plant_id=93): Terai (elevation 60-300m), cultivation_status='marginal', agronomic_suitability='low', regional_cultivation=1, evidence: 'Subsistence/incidental only -- fallow land, field margins; household oil/folk medicine use, not organized commercial farming.' Source: 'Trend Analysis of Oilseed Crops Production in Nepal' (source_id 200, secondary source citing 2013/14 Nepal government statistics).

Season: kharif. No Nepal-specific castor calendar was found; India sources consistently describe sowing Jun-Aug (after monsoon onset) with harvest beginning Dec-Jan for long-duration types, used here as the South Asia default pattern (agrifarming.in; agri.bot sowing-time guide).

Duration: 165 days -- India sources describe improved/long-duration castor varieties maturing in 150-180 days (crop duration '4 to 5 months', sown Jul/Aug, harvest starting Dec/Jan). 165 days is the midpoint of that range; no Nepal-specific variety-duration figure was found, and Nepal's actual subsistence plants (often perennial-ish, multi-picked over a longer informal period) may not follow a single clean cycle in practice.

Cost: NPR 10,000/acre -- ESTIMATE, low confidence. Only a partial India figure was found (weeding ~INR 4,006/ha + spraying ~INR 7,830/ha from a Tamil Nadu study, i.e. only two of many cost line items, not a total). Set below this file's real sesame figure (NPR 17,500/acre) and below the other pulses in this batch, reflecting castor's reputation as an unusually low-maintenance, low-input crop and Nepal's own 'incidental, fallow-land' cultivation pattern implying minimal purchased inputs.

Yield: 3.5 quintal/acre -- ESTIMATE, low confidence, deliberately scaled down from India's own commercial reference figures rather than used directly. India rainfed 'pure crop' castor yields ~1800 kg/ha (~728 kg/acre = 7.28 quintal/acre) and irrigated pure crop ~3000 kg/ha under organized commercial cultivation (castoroil.in); an outlier hybrid figure of up to 8000 kg/ha was excluded as unrepresentative best-case. Since Nepal's real cultivation is explicitly 'subsistence/incidental' rather than organized commercial planting, 3.5 quintal/acre (roughly half the India rainfed commercial reference) was chosen to avoid overstating what a Nepal grower actually achieves -- this downward adjustment is a judgment call, not a citation.

Price: NPR 9,500-11,500/quintal -- ESTIMATE, medium-low confidence, India-anchored. India castor seed mandi price ~INR 6,625/quintal (~INR 62.92/kg) as of Jun 2026 (bankbazaar.com/commodityonline). Converting at the 1.6 peg gives ~NPR 10,600/quintal, which this range brackets.

Sanity check: implied B:C = 3.5 x avg(9500,11500) / 10000 = 3.68 -- inside the 1.5-4 target band and close to this file's real lentil (~3.7). Note this required deliberately discounting the India commercial yield reference (see Yield note) -- an earlier draft using the undiscounted India rainfed yield (7.28 quintal/acre) produced B:C ~7.7, a clear outlier flagged and corrected per this project's known per-acre/per-hectare and best-case/realistic-case bug pattern.

enterprises.name: Niger Seed (Ramtil)
notes: Real, DB-confirmed Mid-Hills oilseed grown on marginal/sub-marginal poor acidic hillside land along the east-west highway -- no released Nepal variety exists yet, meaning what's grown is entirely unimproved/landrace
Price is the best-grounded figure in this entry: India has an active, current (2025-26) government MSP for this exact crop, used as a calibration anchor
Genuinely one of the lowest-input crops on this list -- broadcast-sown with little to no fertilizer, tolerates poor soils that reject most other crops
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database. plant_region_suitability rows (plant_id=94): Mid-Hills (elevation 1000-2000m), cultivation_status='cultivated', agronomic_suitability='high', regional_cultivation=1, evidence: 'Marginal/sub-marginal poor acidic hillside land, along the east-west highway; no released variety yet exists.'; Terai (elevation 60-300m), cultivation_status='marginal', agronomic_suitability='low', regional_cultivation=1, evidence: 'Secondary presence.' No Nepal-specific calendar found; general South Asian niger cultivation guides describe sowing right after the first monsoon rains (Jun-Jul, broadcast onto moist soil) with a short-to-medium cycle -- consistent with the DB's 'poor acidic hillside land' low-input framing. Duration 100 days is a representative South-Asia-typical niger maturity figure, not a Nepal-specific citation.

No hard India or Nepal Rs/ha figure was found, only consistent qualitative statements that niger/ramtil 'requires low investment' and is grown by broadcast-sowing onto poor land with minimal purchased inputs (subsistencefarming.in). Set below this file's real sesame figure (NPR 17,500/acre, itself already a low-input marginal-land oilseed) to reflect niger's reputation as even lower-input than sesame.

Both sources agree in the same 1.2-3 quintal/acre band; 2.0 quintal/acre ('normal' practice) was chosen as the central, realistic figure. Medium confidence -- India-sourced, no direct Nepal yield figure found.

Price: NPR 13,500-15,500/quintal -- the best-grounded price in this batch. India's 2025-26 kharif MSP for niger seed (ramtil) is INR 9,537/quintal, a INR 820 increase over the prior year and the largest absolute MSP increase of any 2025-26 kharif crop (PIB press release, cross-checked against a separate Feb 2026 mandi-price snapshot of INR 8,949.45/quintal, commodityonline.com). Converting the MSP at the fixed 1.6 peg gives ~NPR 15,259/quintal and the mandi price gives ~NPR 14,319/quintal; this range brackets both. An older, much lower 'market price around 4,000 rupees per quintal' figure found in one source was judged stale/superseded by the current MSP and mandi data and was NOT used.
Sanity check: implied B:C = 2.0 x avg(13500,15500) / 9000 = 3.22 -- inside the 1.5-4 target band, similar to this file's real lentil (~3.7).

enterprises.name: Button Mushroom

economics.unit: acre-equivalent (converted from a per-substrate-bag growing-shed basis -- see notes)

notes: Forced per-acre conversion: real button mushroom cultivation happens in a shed on compost-filled bags, not open land. Economics below scale a realistic ~500-bag smallholder shed (500 bags x ~NPR 140/bag = NPR 70,000 total cost; 500 x 1.2kg = 600kg = 6.0 quintal total yield) up to an 'acre-equivalent' by dividing by maxAreaAcre (0.12) -- gram's scoring engine then caps actual land used at 0.12 acre (Math.min(areaAcre, maxAreaAcre)), so this never gets scaled to a literal open acre of mushroom shed.

Needs a cool microclimate (12-18C optimal per the underlying agronomic data) to fruit without mechanical cooling -- Kathmandu Valley's mid-hills winter is specifically what makes it viable there without heavy cooling investment. Seasons restricted to rabi (winter) for this reason, unlike oyster mushroom which spans all three.

Higher capital/skill requirement than oyster (compost preparation + casing soil + closer temperature control), consistent with it remaining a small share (~10%) of Nepal's mushroom production despite a real price premium over oyster.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plants id=132; plant_environment_requirements: temperature 12-18C optimal, up to 28C max, confidence 0.6; plant_region_suitability + regional_crops: Mid-Hills, 'possible'/'high' suitability, ~10% of national mushroom production concentrated in Kathmandu Valley (Balambu/Matatirtha/Thankot) -- Kathmandu Post, 'Mushroom farming: from cultural taboo to a thriving enterprise,' Jan 2025).

Cost: WEB, medium-low confidence. No button-specific Nepal per-bag cost study was found. Base figure is a Nepal-specific generic (largely straw/oyster-style) mushroom cultivation cost of ~NPR 9,000 per 100 bags (NPR 90/bag: straw, spawn, bags/lime/fuel, labor/electricity/rent) from Sewapoint's 2025/26 Nepal mushroom farming guide. Button needs compost + casing soil + more temperature control, so cost/bag was scaled up ~1.5x to NPR 140/bag as this app's own judgment-call estimate for the added inputs -- not a directly cited button-specific figure. Total NPR 70,000 for a 500-bag shed, divided by maxAreaAcre (0.12) = NPR 583,000 acre-equivalent.

Yield: WEB. 1.2 kg/bag assumed (Sewapoint's general 1-1.5kg/bag straw-cultivation range, nudged slightly above the oyster baseline; a separate India ICAR economics page on environment-controlled button cultivation cites ~2kg/bag, suggesting 1.2kg/bag may be conservative). 500 bags x 1.2kg = 600kg = 6.0 quintal, divided by 0.12 acre = 50 quintal acre-equivalent.

Price: WEB, Nepal-specific. NPR 400-450/kg (NPR 40,000-45,000/quintal) -- Kalimati wholesale rate for button mushroom per Sewapoint's 2025/26 guide. A separate Tridge data point puts 'fresh white mushroom' at NPR 290/kg (17 Jan 2025), lower than the Kalimati figure; both are real data points, and this entry uses the more specific, more recent Kalimati-sourced one.

Implied B:C ratio (~3.6) is above both this file's normal field-crop range (1.2-4) and a Nepal-specific academic anchor: a Chitwan, Nepal button-mushroom cost-benefit study found B:C=2.54 (Acharya et al., 'Economic analysis of mushroom enterprise in Chitwan district, Nepal,' Archives of Agriculture and Environmental Science). The gap likely reflects this entry's lean, direct-materials-only cost basis (a farmer-facing guide, not a full cost-accounting survey with imputed labor/land rent) versus Kalimati urban wholesale pricing rather than rural farm-gate pricing. Documented honestly rather than forced down to match field-crop norms, per this batch's explicit brief.

Duration: WEB (general, not Nepal-specific). 90 days assumed for a full compost-to-last-flush cycle -- cultivation guides cite ~10-15 weeks compost-to-steam-off, or ~8-10 weeks from spawning if compost is bought in pre-made (Krishijagran/Agrifarming compost-cultivation guides).

enterprises.name: Oyster Mushroom

economics.unit: acre-equivalent (converted from a per-substrate-bag growing-shed basis -- see notes)

notes: Forced per-acre conversion, same methodology as the other two mushrooms in this batch: a realistic ~500-bag smallholder shed (500 bags x NPR 90/bag = NPR 45,000 total cost; 500 x 1.1kg = 550kg = 5.5 quintal total yield) is scaled up to an 'acre-equivalent' by dividing by maxAreaAcre (0.15). maxAreaAcre is capped at 0.15 acre -- slightly higher than button/shiitake, reflecting oyster's simpler, most-scalable-for-smallholders status -- so the engine never suggests a literal open acre of shed.

Nepal's dominant mushroom by far (~86% of national commercial output, ~35,000 farmers across 47 districts) because it's the cheapest and simplest to grow: straw substrate, no compost/casing, and it tolerates a wider temperature range than button.

Different Pleurotus species/strains suit different seasons (cooler-climate P. ostreatus vs warmer-climate P. sajor-caju, per the underlying agronomic data), so unlike button/shiitake this entry is marked eligible in all three seasons rather than winter-only.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plants id=131; plant_environment_requirements: temperature range 5-30C depending on species/strain -- 'P.ostreatus 5-20C (winter), P.sajor-caju 25-30C (summer)', confidence 0.6; plant_region_suitability + regional_crops: Mid-Hills 'most favorable zone overall,' Terai 'grown mainly in cooler months there,' both 'possible'/'high' suitability -- Kathmandu Post, 'Mushroom farming: from cultural taboo to a thriving enterprise,' Jan 2025).

Cost: WEB, Nepal-specific, medium confidence. NPR 9,000 per 100 straw bags (NPR 90/bag: straw, spawn, bags/lime/fuel, labor/electricity/rent) -- Sewapoint's 2025/26 Nepal mushroom farming guide, a small-farmer-oriented direct-materials estimate (current and Nepal-specific, but a farming guide rather than an audited cost study). Scaled to a 500-bag shed (NPR 45,000) and divided by maxAreaAcre (0.15) = NPR 300,000 acre-equivalent.
Yield: same Sewapoint source -- 1.1 kg/bag (100-120kg per 100-bag batch). 500 bags x 1.1kg = 550kg = 5.5 quintal, divided by 0.15 acre = 36.7 quintal acre-equivalent.

Price: WEB, Nepal-specific, high confidence for this batch. NPR 250-300/kg (NPR 25,000-30,000/quintal) -- Sewapoint's Nepal guide ('online Kathmandu rates'), independently cross-checked against Tridge's 'fresh king oyster mushroom' Nepal price of NPR 290/kg (17 Jan 2025). Two independent Nepal-specific sources converge closely.

Implied B:C ratio (~3.4) is above this file's normal field-crop range (1.2-4) and above a general oyster-mushroom B:C figure of 1.31-1.79 found in the wider literature during this search (region/provenance of that specific figure unclear from search snippets, plausibly India rather than Nepal) -- likely for the same reason noted under button mushroom (leaner cost basis, urban wholesale pricing here vs a fuller cost-accounting basis there). Documented rather than forced down, per this batch's brief.

Duration: ~45 days (10-14 day spawn run + 5-7 days to first flush = ~25 days to first harvest, plus 2-3 further flushes over the following ~3 weeks before a bag is exhausted) -- Sewapoint Nepal guide cycle timeline.

enterprises.name: Shiitake Mushroom

economics.unit: acre-equivalent (converted from a per-substrate-block growing-shed basis -- see notes)

notes: LOWEST-CONFIDENCE entry in this batch alongside lucerne. Forced per-acre conversion, same methodology as the other two mushrooms: a realistic ~300-block smallholder operation (smaller than oyster/button, reflecting shiitake's niche/pilot-scale status in Nepal) costing an estimated NPR 48,000 total and yielding 300kg (3.0 quintal), divided by maxAreaAcre (0.08 -- the smallest cap of the three mushrooms, reflecting a genuinely small real land/shed footprint) to produce the acre-equivalent figures here.

Modeled as sawdust/log-block cultivation (2-4 months inoculation-to-harvest), NOT traditional whole-log cultivation, which is also practiced in Nepal (Alnus/Castonopsis hardwood logs) but takes far longer -- 6-24 months to first harvest, then 2-3 harvests/year over several subsequent years. durationDays=90 reflects the faster block method; a real log-based operation would tie up land/capital far longer than this figure implies -- a genuine simplification, flagged explicitly rather than hidden.

Still a marginal/pilot activity in Nepal (~2% of national mushroom production; small NGO-training-linked operations in Taplejung/Kavre/Lalitpur/Bhaktapur) rather than an established industry -- treat this as the lowest-confidence of the three mushroom entries for that reason, alongside its thin cost/yield data.
Commands a large price premium over button/oyster (roughly 2-3x), which is the main real driver of its unusually high implied B:C ratio below -- not an assumption of higher per-block productivity.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plants id=133; no plant_environment_requirements rows exist for this plant -- expected per this batch's brief, since indoor/substrate-grown mushrooms are thinly represented in a climate-focused schema; plant_region_suitability + regional_crops: Mid-Hills only, 'possible'/'low' suitability, 'marginal' cultivation status, ~2% of national production -- Kathmandu Post, 'Mushroom farming: from cultural taboo to a thriving enterprise,' Jan 2025).

Cost: WEB, low confidence -- no Nepal shiitake per-block cost source was found. Estimated NPR 160/block by analogy to button mushroom's cost premium over oyster (compost/casing-equivalent extra input intensity), loosely cross-checked against an India per-cycle shiitake economics figure (yield 200-400+kg, revenue Rs24,000-120,000+, profit Rs10,000-50,000+ per cycle -- Agrifarming.in) implying a similar order-of-magnitude per-cycle cost once scaled to a per-block basis. This app's own estimate, not a directly cited figure. 300 blocks x NPR 160 = NPR 48,000, divided by maxAreaAcre (0.08) = NPR 600,000 acre-equivalent.

Yield: WEB, low confidence. 1.0 kg/block assumed (conservative; no direct Nepal source; the same India per-cycle reference above is broadly consistent at this scale). 300 blocks x 1.0kg = 300kg = 3.0 quintal, divided by 0.08 acre = 37.5 quintal acre-equivalent.

Price: WEB, Nepal-specific, the best-grounded figure of the three mushrooms despite the thin cost/yield data. NPR 700-1,000/kg fresh (NPR 70,000-100,000/quintal) -- NPR 700-800/kg per Kathmandu Post (also the nepal_agri_ai database's own source id=213) plus a more recent NPR 1,000/kg Kalimati wholesale quote (Ratopati, April 2026). Dried shiitake reaches NPR 2,000/kg but that's a different, non-comparable product form and was not used here.

Implied B:C ratio (~5.3) is the highest and most unusual-looking of the three mushroom entries, driven mainly by shiitake's large price premium (2-3x oyster/button) rather than any assumed high per-block output -- consistent with the literature's framing of shiitake as Nepal's most profitable but least-established mushroom. Flagged as the lowest-confidence numeric entry in this whole batch: real Nepal per-block cost/yield data for shiitake was not found, so cost and yield here are reasoned analogies, not citations.

enterprises.name: Berseem (Egyptian Clover)
notes: Grown on open land like a normal field crop -- no forced land-model conversion needed, unlike the mushrooms in this batch. The real judgment call here is economic: Berseem is very often grown specifically to feed a household's own livestock rather than sold, so the price below should be read as either a real local sale price OR a feed-cost-avoided (substitution) value -- see the price source note for why both interpretations land on the same number.

Classic Terai winter (rabi) fodder legume, sown October-November (often relayed into standing rice), cut roughly every 30 days for 5-6 cuttings through to around May -- durationDays (210) spans this full multi-cut window, not just one cutting.

Needs regular irrigation through the dry winter season (no monsoon rain falls during its growing window) -- marked irrigated-only, unlike the more drought-tolerant fodder crops in this batch (Napier, Stylo).
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plants id=141; plant_environment_requirements: elevation 100-1400m with optimal ~600m, rainfall 550-750mm, soil pH 6.5-8.0, Nepal-specific, confidence 0.4-0.7; regional_crops: Terai, cultivated, 'nearly throughout Terai (Jhapa to Kanchanpur),' seed-production pockets in Dhanusha/Mahottari/Sarlahi/Rautahat/Banke/Bardiya -- Rameshwar Singh Pande, 'Potential for Berseem Seed Production in Nepal,' NARC-sourced content). Zones extended to include hills given the elevation ceiling reaches 1400m into Mid-Hills territory, though the cited regional_crops evidence itself documents Terai only.

Cost: WEB, low-medium confidence -- no direct Nepal berseem fodder-cultivation cost figure was found. Estimated NPR 25,000/acre by analogy to this file's existing irrigated Nepal winter-crop cost (wheat: NPR 27,700/acre), adjusted for multi-cut fodder labor instead of grain harvest/threshing. Cross-checked against an India berseem SEED-production cost of Rs 45,983-62,330/ha (Jhansi, India; converts to roughly NPR 30,000/acre after INR-to-NPR and hectare-to-acre conversion) -- seed production normally costs more than simple fodder-cutting, so this cross-check is directionally consistent with, though not a direct source for, the NPR 25,000/acre figure used.

Yield: WEB (India, not Nepal-specific). 500 quintal/ha green fodder used -- the conservative end of a commonly cited 500-600 quintal/ha range over 5-6 cuttings (some sources cite up to 750-1200 quintal/ha under very good conditions; not used here, to stay conservative) -- eagri.org AGR301 fodder-crop lecture notes; Dairy Knowledge Portal. Converted to 200 quintal/acre (500 / 2.4711 ha-per-acre).

Price: WEB, medium-low confidence, cross-species analogy. NPR 300-400/quintal (NPR 3-4/kg) green fodder. Best available real anchor is a Nepal-specific fodder MAIZE economics figure found in this pass -- average price NPR 345/quintal, average returns NPR 185,955/ha (a Chitwan-district-linked Nepal fodder/silage economics study; exact paper not independently re-verified beyond the search result) -- cross-checked against a general India green-fodder market price of ~Rs 280/quintal (~NPR 448/quintal after INR-to-NPR conversion). Applied to berseem by cross-species analogy since green fodder tends to be priced by bulk/weight rather than species in these informal markets, and no berseem-specific Nepal price was found. Real informal green-fodder markets do exist in Nepal's dairy-intensive Terai, so this can be read as a genuine sale price; where a farmer instead feeds their own berseem to their own livestock, the same figure represents the cost of the purchased fodder they avoid -- flagged explicitly since both readings are plausible and this project did not confirm which applies more often.

enterprises.name: Lucerne (Alfalfa)
notes: LOWEST-CONFIDENCE entry in this batch alongside shiitake_mushroom. Grown on open land -- no land-model conversion needed -- but the underlying nepal_agri_ai research explicitly calls Lucerne 'the weakest-documented of the fodder crops' (a single NARC trial site), and no Nepal-specific cost or price figure was found at all for it.

Zones restricted to high-hills only, deliberately NOT following Lucerne/alfalfa's well-known India pattern of being mainly a Punjab/Haryana PLAINS crop -- the only real Nepal cultivation evidence found is a single high-altitude trans-Himalayan trial (Marpha, Mustang, ~2600m), so this entry follows that Nepal-specific pattern rather than the India lowland analogy.

Perennial multi-cut forage legume like Napier/Stylo in this batch -- durationDays=365 reflects a standing multi-year stand cut repeatedly within its snow-free growing window (roughly April-November at this elevation); seasons exclude rabi (winter) to reflect high-altitude dormancy, a reasoned assumption rather than a directly documented fact.

Yield was deliberately adjusted down from the India figures found (280-320 quintal/acre in intensive Punjab-plains conditions) to reflect Nepal's harsher, shorter-season, rain-shadow high-altitude growing conditions -- a judgment call, not a cited Nepal yield figure.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plants id=142; plant_environment_requirements: elevation up to 2650m at the Marpha trial site, rainfall 200-2500mm range, very wide/low-confidence 'regional fallback,' confidence 0.3-0.6; regional_crops: High Hills, cultivated, 'one NARC trial site at Marpha, Mustang (~2566-2650m, trans-Himalayan rain-shadow valley)' -- explicitly flagged by the source database itself as the weakest-documented fodder crop; Mountain zone marked marginal -- Rameshwar Singh Pande, 'Promising Species for Fodder and Pasture Development in Nepal,' NARC-sourced content).

Cost: WEB, lowest confidence in this batch -- no Nepal or India lucerne cultivation cost figure was found at all. Estimated NPR 22,000/acre by analogy to this batch's other perennial fodder crops (similar order of magnitude to Napier's estimate, adjusted slightly for likely higher input-transport costs at a remote high-hill site like Marpha). This app's own unverified estimate.

Yield: WEB (India). Sources report a wide range -- 400-600 quintal/ha (80-120 quintal/ha dry matter) in general references, and 80-150 t/ha in specific variety trials; one figure already in per-acre terms ('7-8 cuttings, average fodder yield of 280 to 320 quintals per acre') -- eagri.org AGR301 lecture notes; Agrifarming.in. That figure was adjusted down to 150 quintal/acre here to reflect Nepal's high-altitude rain-shadow growing conditions versus the intensive irrigated Indian-plains conditions it was measured under -- a judgment call, explicitly not a Nepal-specific yield figure.

Price: WEB, medium-low confidence, cross-species analogy. Same NPR 300-400/quintal green-fodder market/substitution-value basis used for berseem/Napier/Stylo (see berseem's price source note for the underlying Nepal fodder-maize and India green-fodder anchors) -- applied here by the same cross-species analogy, with even lower confidence than the other three since Lucerne's only documented Nepal presence is a single research trial, not an established farmer market.

enterprises.name: Napier Grass
notes: Grown on open land -- no land-model conversion needed. Perennial grass: once established, it's cut repeatedly through the year rather than planted-and-harvested-once, so durationDays=365 and all three seasons are marked eligible.

Genuinely low-input relative to the other fodder crops here -- tolerates marginal land (grown on bunds/terrace risers/wasteland per the underlying Nepal data) and needs comparatively little irrigation, reflected in both its lower waterDependency risk score and its inclusion of rainfed alongside irrigated.

Yield figures in the wider literature vary enormously (roughly 12-45+ t/ha) depending on whether a source is reporting dry-matter or fresh/green weight, and on rainfall/management intensity -- this entry explicitly uses a fresh/green-weight basis (matching this file's yieldUnitLabel convention elsewhere) and a mid-range, smallholder-realistic figure rather than the highest experimental-plot numbers found; see yield source note.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plants id=140; plant_environment_requirements: temperature minimum 15C (growth halts below), optimal 25-40C, elevation ceiling 1500m, Nepal-specific; regional_crops: Terai (7,903 ha nationally per NLSIP), Inner Terai (bunds/terrace risers/wasteland), Mid-Hills up to ~1500m (Nawalparasi, Gorkha, Kavre, Kaski) -- NLSIP/MoALD, 'Assessment of Feed Resources, Feeding Practices, Nutritional Status' (nlsip.gov.np)).

Cost: WEB, low-medium confidence -- no Nepal or India Napier cultivation cost figure was found (multiple searches returned agronomic/yield detail but explicitly no cost breakdown). Estimated NPR 25,000/acre/year, reasoned upward from an initial low-input assumption once repeated-cutting harvest labor was accounted for (Napier is cut 4-6+ times/year, and manually cutting/carrying ~180 quintal/acre/year of fibrous stalks is real recurring labor even though the crop itself needs little irrigation or replanting). Cross-checked for order-of-magnitude plausibility against the Nepal fodder-maize economics used for berseem's price (~NPR 75,000/acre revenue at BCR>1, see berseem's price source) -- since Napier is perennial (no annual reseeding/land-prep, unlike fodder maize) its cost should run below fodder maize's, which this figure does. This app's own estimate, not a directly cited figure.

Yield: WEB (India-focused, not Nepal-specific). Reports found ranged from 12-25 t/ha dry matter (up to 40+ t/ha DM in high-rainfall areas) to a separately-reported 45 t/ha/year without a clearly stated basis (Krishijagran/eKishaan/agricultural-extension sources). This entry treats that 45 t/ha figure as fresh/green weight and applies it directly (45 / 2.4711 ha-per-acre = ~182, rounded to 180 quintal/acre) rather than the dry-matter figures -- flagged explicitly because sources found were inconsistent about which basis they used.

Price: WEB, medium-low confidence, cross-species analogy. Same NPR 300-400/quintal green-fodder market/substitution-value basis as berseem (see berseem's price source note for the underlying Nepal fodder-maize and India green-fodder anchors).

enterprises.name: Stylo
notes: Grown on open land -- no land-model conversion needed. Deep-rooted, drought-tolerant perennial legume, valued specifically for staying green through the dry season -- marked eligible in all three seasons and given the lowest risk scores of any entry in this batch (low price volatility, low water dependency, low capital lock-in), reflecting its real role as a low-input, marginal-land subsistence forage rather than a market cash crop.

Notably broad soil tolerance, including acidic and low-fertility soils that most other fodder/field crops in this file would not tolerate -- explicitly documented in the underlying research as a reason it's used for revegetating degraded steep mid-hill land, not just as ordinary pasture.

The yield figure below was deliberately adjusted down from what a Nepal-specific source literally states (see yield source) because the raw converted number looked implausibly high next to a broadly comparable grass-legume figure (Napier) in this same batch -- flagged explicitly as a plausibility judgment call, not a rejection of the source.
sources: Agronomic data: nepal_agri_ai database (plants id=143; plant_environment_requirements: elevation ceiling 1500m, soil pH 4.0-8.3 -- 'tolerates acidic/low-fertility soils better than most fodder crops,' Nepal-specific, confidence 0.4-0.6; regional_crops: Terai ('up to 1200-1500m,' consistently cited), Mid-Hills ('Palpa Stylo' is NARC's recommended variety, feeding trial at Gorkha 1097m, 'heavily used for silvi-pasture/rehabilitation of degraded steep mid-hill land') -- IJAST/DesTech Publications, 'Effect of Stylo Grass Supplement on Khari Goats, Mid-Hills of Nepal,' 2013).

Cost: WEB, low-medium confidence -- no Nepal or India Stylo cultivation cost figure was found. Estimated NPR 15,000/acre/year, the lowest of the four fodder crops in this batch, reflecting Stylo's documented role as a hardy, low-maintenance legume for marginal/degraded land (little or no fertilizer, no irrigation infrastructure, minimal purchased inputs) rather than an intensively managed crop. This app's own estimate, not a directly cited figure.

Yield: WEB, Nepal-specific source with an explicit downward adjustment. A Nepal source states 'total green fodder yield of about 5 metric tons per ropani across the four cuts' (cgspace.cgiar.org, 'Extension materials on fodder management for the Mid-hills of Nepal'). Converted literally (1 ropani = 508.72 sqm; 1 acre = 7.955 ropani) this is ~398 quintal/acre -- more than double this batch's Napier grass estimate, which is implausible for a legume against a fast-growing C4 fodder grass. This entry uses a deliberately discounted 150 quintal/acre instead, on the judgment that the source figure (or this unit conversion) is more likely an outlier than that Stylo genuinely out-yields Napier -- flagged explicitly as a downward adjustment, not a cited figure.
Price: WEB, medium-low confidence, cross-species analogy. Same NPR 300-400/quintal green-fodder market/substitution-value basis as berseem/Napier/Lucerne (see berseem's price source note).
